stamp.assurance_means: the hashed bytes are exactly the text the models were given

front_matter.title: Marian M1 design critique: per-expert VRAM residency on upstream llama.cpp
front_matter.problem: Marian is a thin fork of the latest llama.cpp (pin a37cc461, 21 Oct 2026) that must lift the VRAM expert hit rate of a large MoE model on constrained laptops from about 33% (stock whole-layer placement) to about 85% (Strata's measured figure), exact by default, self-calibrating to any machine. DESIGN-M1.md proposes building on upstream's new --moe-cache-mib cache. Find its defects AND tell us how to make it faster.
front_matter.in_scope: The design in DESIGN-M1.md: architecture, the patch set on llama.cpp, the layer on top, the calibration loop, the exactness contract and its tests, the measurement protocol, milestones, risks, open decisions. Performance: every way the design leaves decode, prefill or hit rate on the table on 8-16 GB VRAM / 16-32 GB RAM laptops.
front_matter.out_of_scope: Whether Marian should exist; Chris's four decisions (thin fork on latest llama.cpp; exact by default with opt-in answer-changing switches; built on the reference laptop by Claude Tyl; self-calibrating, not tuned for one machine). Style and wording.
front_matter.context: Reference laptop: RTX 4090 Laptop 16 GB, i7-13700HX AVX2, 32 GB DDR5, Windows 11, NVMe. Model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Swift 1.5 IQ2_XS (qwen4exp, 48 layers, 512 experts, 10 used, 33.02 GiB routed experts in three layouts, 26.82 GiB lazily read PLE table). Strata: 35.5 tok/s decode median, 85.4% hit from 9.16 GiB, with MTP, route-tail skip and CPU/GPU split. Stock llama.cpp -ncmoe 32: 7-10.6 tok/s. The research pack has the citations. Nothing in the design has been run on the new pin.
known_decisions: Exact mode means bitwise identical to the same build with every expert in VRAM of the same GPU (section 3). Answer-changing mechanisms are opt-in; do not report their being off by default as a defect.
Build on upstream llama-moe-cache.cpp rather than port Strata's engine (recommended to Chris, section 12.1). Arguments against it are welcome if they are concrete.
No GPU benchmarks were run for this design; the numbers marked estimate are arithmetic.
Marian launches upstream llama-server bound to 127.0.0.1; no server of its own.
front_matter.access_rules: Read-only design material and public MIT source. No secrets, no personal data in any file. Do not print credentials or e-mail addresses if you meet any.
front_matter.severity_scale: Critical = the design cannot meet M1 (85% hit, exact, decode >= 12 tok/s) or breaks exactness; High = a large performance loss or a wrong measurement conclusion likely; Medium = a real but bounded loss or gap; Low = minor.

critiques.summary: The design identifies the right upstream cache and tests its numerical path early, but three gaps threaten its stated outcome: M1 requires a decode floor before it fixes disk-backed misses; its governor cannot release VRAM from upstream’s fixed bank allocation; and the proposed cache instrumentation misses large-batch prefill. The later expert sidecar also needs a stronger content identity to preserve exactness.

findings.title: A metadata-matched sidecar could silently serve weights from a different model
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §6.2 keys the routing profile by “a content hash of every shard’s tensor-info table and expert offsets”; §4 proposes an optional expert-major sidecar, and §5 P3 makes it a source of expert bytes. RESEARCH-PACK.md §3 says the current fill instead copies bytes from the model tensor at llama-moe-cache.cpp:591-605.
findings.failure_scenario: A fine-tuned or replaced GGUF has identical tensor names, shapes and offsets but different expert payloads. If the derived sidecar uses the proposed identity, it can still appear to belong to that model and supply the old weights. Checksums of sidecar records alone would establish only that the sidecar is internally intact.
findings.why_it_matters: This changes logits while the feature is classified as exact; routing-profile misidentification alone would only hurt placement, but reusing expert *bytes* breaks the contract.
findings.fix: Give derived byte sources a separate, verified full-payload identity for every source shard, or a trusted manifest of payload hashes. Bind each sidecar record to its original tensor bytes, build and publish sidecars atomically, and refuse the sidecar on any mismatch. A metadata hash remains suitable as a layout key, not a byte-identity key.

findings.title: The M1 governor cannot reclaim the bank VRAM it promises to shrink
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §7.7 promises to “shrink the adaptive region by whole slots” under competing allocations, and M1.3 requires no collapse under one. In llama-moe-cache.cpp:343-365 slot counts are set at construction; :388-470 constructs the banks and allocates one buffer per device. Bank lending or release/rebuild work is deferred to P7 in §5, M5.
findings.failure_scenario: Another application takes VRAM after server start. Removing entries from SLRU changes logical occupancy, not the size of the allocated bank buffer. The proposed M1 governor reports fewer usable slots while the GPU allocation, and thus the spill or OOM pressure, remains.
findings.why_it_matters: The measured reference-laptop cliff is sharp: RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 reports 10.59 to 3.56 tok/s decode across adjacent configurations. M1.3’s competing-allocation exit test cannot be satisfied by the described shrink operation.
findings.fix: Either implement and test physical bank release/reallocation plus graph rebinding before M1.3, or specify a stop-and-restart/replan governor and change the exit test accordingly. Until then, call logical admission throttling a hit-rate policy, not VRAM reclamation.

findings.title: PERF: Move bounded expert sourcing ahead of the M1 decode exit
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §10 puts P3’s RAM tier, staging and unbuffered tail in M2, after M1’s ≥12 tok/s exit; §11 already identifies RAM/NVMe misses as a high-likelihood limit. Until P3, llama-moe-cache.cpp:591-605 fills from w->data. RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 reports roughly 19 GiB initially free host RAM against a roughly 23.86 GiB expert complement at Strata-sized VRAM residency, and an older stock run falling from 10.59 to 4.86 tok/s after long prefill.
findings.failure_scenario: P2 attains 85% VRAM hits, but the roughly 15% remaining selections—about 99 MiB of expert bytes per token using the pack’s 660 MiB figure—fault from an unmanaged mmap after prefill. At an illustrative 2 GiB/s of exposed disk service, those bytes alone take about 48 ms per token, before GPU work, uploads and request latency. P2 cannot fix that source.
findings.why_it_matters: The 12 tok/s floor is an 83 ms/token budget. The older stock run does not prove a new-pin outcome, but the design makes its throughput exit depend on a source-tier repair scheduled only afterward.
findings.fix: Put a minimal P3 demand path—bounded RAM, pinned staging, explicit queued tail reads, and measurement in both copy paths—before the M1 throughput exit; defer sidecar and predictive I/O if needed. Patch llama.cpp’s fill and selective-copy source hooks, with tier management in Marian. This is byte-preserving/exact if source identity is verified. Estimated gain is 0 when pages remain resident, but potentially recovery from a roughly 2× post-prefill slowdown when paging is causal; measure it on the new pin.

findings.title: P5b gives the host no timely way to service a tail miss before the GPU waits for it
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P5b says the GPU resolves misses in-stream, “admission happens between tokens from a device-side miss ring,” and tail misses “wait on a mapped flag.” §7 explicitly expects NVMe tails on smaller RAM machines.
findings.failure_scenario: A selected expert is absent from the mapped pinned tier. The GPU reaches its flag wait during a layer, but the described host drain of the miss ring occurs only between tokens—after that layer and token can finish. The request times out or stalls unless there is a separate, intra-token publication and service protocol that the design does not specify.
findings.why_it_matters: A timeout below WDDM’s TDR is not a successful exact fallback. Cold experts are normal on a 16 GB RAM machine, so this is not an exceptional-only path if P5b is selected.
findings.fix: Prefer P5a for the tail initially. For P5b, specify a demand ID publication before the wait, a concurrently running host reader, system-scope ordering of ID/data/ready flags, completion and error propagation, and a tested timeout fallback that still computes the requested expert. Test forced cold misses and I/O failures, not just resident-tier parity.

findings.title: P1 and P4 cannot observe the large-batch prefill they claim to profile
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 locates P1’s selected-ID trace in llama-moe-cache.cpp copy():549-617 and P4’s separate prefill/decode counts in llama-moe-cache.cpp. But get_slot_map() returns null when n_tokens > 32 (llama-moe-cache.cpp:496-507); large batches instead take the selective-copy path described in RESEARCH-PACK.md §3 at llama-context.cpp:2788-2859. copy_experts() at llama-moe-cache.cpp:514-547 sees copied ranges, not the full per-token selection trace.
findings.failure_scenario: The 20k-token mixed calibration corpus includes long documents, but normal pp512/pp4096 ubatches bypass P1’s proposed callback. Its prefill histogram and persisted prefill counts are absent or biased toward small batches, so replay and phase-specific plans can look validated while predicting the wrong prefill demand.
findings.why_it_matters: M1.1 requires replay to predict upstream within three points; M1.3 then sizes tiers from that profile. Missing an entire execution path invalidates those checks, not merely a dashboard.
findings.fix: Trace selected IDs at a point shared by both paths, or instrument llama-context.cpp’s selective-copy callback as well. Preserve token/row association and phase labels; assert in tests that a pp4096 run records its expected layer selections before accepting replay accuracy.

findings.title: The model-free, 256 MiB VRAM cliff probe is too coarse to certify a serving budget
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §6.1 proposes 256 MiB allocation steps and a >3× bandwidth-collapse trigger, mostly without the model; §7.4 subtracts predicted dense, KV and workspace usage from that result. RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 reports the observed sharp change between approximately 16,018 and 16,040 MiB—22 MiB apart—and notes that server/16K serving headroom was not measured (§10, question 8).
findings.failure_scenario: The probe crosses a narrow budget or hits allocation failure without satisfying its bandwidth trigger. Its small copy/matmul also need not reproduce a loaded server’s workspace peaks, allocation layout, growing KV, display use or concurrent application. The plan marks a bank safe but serving spills during prefill or context growth.
findings.why_it_matters: The failure is several-fold throughput loss without an OOM, precisely what self-calibration is meant to prevent. A subtractive model is useful for candidates, not sufficient validation.
findings.fix: Treat the standalone probe as a bound. Validate finalists with the loaded model at requested context and peak ubatch, repeat near the boundary at finer increments, handle OOM as a cliff signal, and test controlled competing allocations. Record headroom over the full request, not only startup or depth-zero decode.

findings.title: The Swift tests cannot establish the stated whole-model all-resident reference
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.1 defines exactness against every Swift routed expert resident on the same GPU. RESEARCH-PACK.md addendum gives 33.02 GiB of Swift routed experts versus the reference GPU’s 16 GB. DESIGN-M1.md §3.6 therefore substitutes single-layer E0, a different fitting model in E2, and Swift cache-versus-selective-copy E2b.
findings.failure_scenario: E0 passes for frozen inputs and E2b agrees with another offload path, yet a Swift-specific graph operation, batch shape or bank-dependent dispatch differs from a true all-resident Swift graph. Neither surrogate runs the defined whole-model reference on the reference GPU.
findings.why_it_matters: The tests are useful necessary checks, but labeling E0–E2b a proof of the literal Swift contract overstates what they can establish.
findings.fix: State the reference as a per-operation equivalence obligation on the reference GPU, including all Swift layouts and relevant row counts, and document the remaining compositional assumption. Add whole-Swift all-resident comparisons on a sufficiently large GPU of the same architecture where available; do not present that other GPU as a literal same-GPU test for the laptop.

findings.title: Upstream hit counters count distinct experts, not the proposed per-row lookup denominator
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §9.2 specifies hits divided by 480 lookups per decode token and comparisons involving verify windows. In llama-moe-cache.cpp:109-152, plan() de-duplicates IDs into uniq and increments n_hit once per distinct resident expert; :608-611 records n_hit and fills.size(). RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 identifies Strata’s 85.4% as 75,318/88,222 observed lookups, while DESIGN-M1.md §9.2 uses a median per-token statistic for its exit.
findings.failure_scenario: Two rows in one verify ubatch request the same resident expert. Upstream records one hit, while a lookup-based metric records two. Reusing those counters for P1 or replay understates row hits; independently, a median of Marian’s tokens is not directly comparable to Strata’s aggregate on another workload.
findings.why_it_matters: Policy comparisons, the three-point replay check and the advertised ‘85% versus 85.4%’ can reach different conclusions depending on which denominator is used. Single-token decode has ten distinct selected experts per layer, so this particular de-duplication error is chiefly a batched-path issue.
findings.fix: Record both distinct fills/copies and row-level demand hits, snapshotting residency before each ubatch’s fills and attributing rows to tokens. Report aggregate and per-token distributions side by side, and use matched workloads before comparing with Strata’s aggregate.

findings.title: PERF: Avoid making the entire ranked warm fill a first-token barrier
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §4 fills the ranked core “before the first token,” and §10 targets roughly Strata-sized residency. RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 gives that size as 9.16 GiB; §9.2 measures first-token time, but the plan does not distinguish the cost of a cold profile fill from inference.
findings.failure_scenario: On a cold start, preloading up to 9.16 GiB can require several seconds of NVMe reads before even a short prompt starts. The start looks fast only in warm-file-cache runs; a user with a short request pays to load experts it will not visit.
findings.why_it_matters: This leaves TTFT on the table even if steady-state decode and hit rate meet M1.
findings.fix: In P2 and Marian’s launch plan, test a tiered warm start: synchronously load a small, high-value core, then fill remaining ranked slots only from available I/O and VRAM capacity while serving demand. Keep demand priority and lease-safe publication. This is exact because only residency changes. At an illustrative 2 GiB/s cold read rate, deferring 8 GiB could remove up to about 4 seconds of startup I/O from a short request; steady-state gain may be zero, so gate it on measured TTFT and subsequent hit loss.

brief_challenges.challenge: The brief pairs an 85% Marian median per-token exit with Strata’s 85.4% aggregate lookup result as though they were the same target.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: DESIGN-M1.md §9.2 and RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 use different aggregation and workloads. Require both statistics on matched requests before claiming to have replicated Strata’s hit result.

brief_challenges.challenge: The literal same-GPU, all-experts-in-VRAM Swift reference is physically unavailable on the specified 16 GB laptop.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: Swift routed experts alone occupy 33.02 GiB (RESEARCH-PACK.md addendum). The brief should distinguish an operational per-layer parity contract from an unattainable whole-model local reference.

brief_challenges.challenge: ‘Self-calibrating to any machine’ needs an explicit unsupported-or-degraded outcome, not just smaller planned tiers.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: The brief includes 8 GB VRAM and 16 GB RAM machines while the model has 33.02 GiB of expert weights. Calibration can measure an infeasible latency or memory budget; success criteria should say when Marian warns or refuses rather than implying it can always select a useful plan.

done_well: The design checks the new upstream cache before attributing stock-versus-Strata gains to Marian.
E0 tests forced misses, permuted slots and reuse before performance work; the MMVQ/MMQ row-count boundary is explicitly recognized.
The design keeps CPU computation and route-tail skipping out of exact mode and treats miss-source latency, not hit rate alone, as a performance objective.
could_not_verify: No GPU measurements at the pinned commit establish SLRU hit rate, synchronization cost, post-prefill throughput or the proposed performance gains.
The supplied source does not include an implementation of P1–P9, the sidecar identity checks, or the P5b host/device demand protocol.

critiques.summary: The design is directionally strong and appropriately treats the upstream cache as an exactness hypothesis to test, not a proven result. Two implementation risks need resolution before relying on the plan: P5(a) specifies a wait for the bank matmul but not for the earlier slot-map lookup, and the governor’s proposed logical cache shrink does not release the upstream cache’s fixed-size bank allocation. The exact-by-default policy is also unresolved for non-bitwise speculation; direct-I/O alignment, profile identity, row-count parity coverage, and non-reference hardware validation need more detail. No performance claim has been measured on the pin.

findings.title: P5(a) gates the matmul but not the earlier slot-map lookup
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5, P5(a), specifies that “the bank op waits on a copy-complete event.” In the existing graph, `GET_ROWS` reads the slot map before `MUL_MAT_ID` (`llama-graph.cpp:2582-2621`); the cache callback publishes the updated map after fills (`llama-moe-cache.cpp:611-614`).
findings.failure_scenario: If the worker publishes the new map asynchronously and the graph reaches `GET_ROWS` first, that lookup can produce a slot from the previous mapping. If that slot was evicted and now contains another expert, waiting before the matmul only ensures the new bytes are present; it cannot correct the already-read slot ID. This can silently produce wrong logits.
findings.why_it_matters: P5(a) is classified as exact, but correct bank bytes are insufficient unless the slot-map version used by `GET_ROWS` is also ordered with the policy update.
findings.fix: Make `GET_ROWS` wait for map publication, separately from the bank-fill dependency before `MUL_MAT_ID`. Use versioned or double-buffered maps and leases so the map and bank contents refer to the same generation. Stress-test delayed map uploads, misses, evictions, and slot reuse.

findings.title: The VRAM governor shrinks residency, not the allocated bank
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §7 step 7 says to “shrink the adaptive region by whole slots” when another program takes memory. Upstream creates banks with a fixed `n_slots + 1` shape and allocates their backend buffer at construction (`llama-moe-cache.cpp:304-312, 436-453`); P2 also sets slot counts before bank creation (`DESIGN-M1.md §5`).
findings.failure_scenario: Another process consumes VRAM after Marian starts. Pausing admission or marking fewer slots usable leaves the already allocated bank occupying the same VRAM, so the WDDM budget remains exceeded and the process can still spill, collapse in speed, or fail a later allocation.
findings.why_it_matters: The design relies on the governor to protect against the observed WDDM cliff, but logical eviction alone does not return memory to the driver.
findings.fix: Implement actual bank resizing or segmented allocations that can be released after draining all readers, then update views, slot maps, and scheduler bindings safely. If that cannot be done, use a conservative fixed budget and reject or pause requests rather than claiming runtime shrink will restore headroom.

findings.title: The parity gate does not specify coverage for the disclosed row-count cliffs
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.3 describes different paths at 7, 8, and 9 rows. E0 in §3 specifies one layer of each layout with frozen activations but no row-count sweep; E1 specifies held-out teacher-forced and generated tokens but does not enumerate batch shapes. The exactness definition in §3.1 itself fixes `n_batch` and `n_ubatch` because row count affects the path.
findings.failure_scenario: A single-token decode parity run can pass while an 8- or 9-row verify batch, or a different prefill ubatch, selects a different kernel or bank dispatch and diverges. The test plan would then have certified only the exercised shapes, not the supported configurations implied by the exactness contract.
findings.why_it_matters: The design explicitly identifies row count and bank shape as numerical risks, but the merge gate does not state how those risks are covered.
findings.fix: Make the parity matrix explicit: test representative row counts including 1, 7, 8, 9, 32, and the large-batch selective-copy path; cover all three layouts, relevant bank sizes, and actual prefill ubatches. Compare intermediate expert outputs as well as logits.

findings.title: The unbuffered GGUF read path omits required alignment handling
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §4 and §5 P3 propose `FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING` / `O_DIRECT` reads of cold expert ranges from GGUF shards. Fable’s `ideas/fable-ideas.md`, Idea 4, notes that GGUF expert offsets are 32-byte aligned and calls for sector-rounded reads with trimming; that requirement is not specified in the design’s source interface.
findings.failure_scenario: A cold expert slice starts or ends at an offset not accepted by the filesystem/device’s direct-I/O alignment rules. The read fails (for example, with an invalid-parameter/alignment error), or a fallback silently returns to buffered mmap I/O and reintroduces page-cache pressure.
findings.why_it_matters: The tail-read path is intended to control the very paging and latency variability that the design identifies as a bottleneck, and it must work on both Windows and Linux.
findings.fix: Define per-platform alignment discovery and an aligned bounce buffer: round file ranges outward to the required sector/block boundary, issue aligned reads, then copy only the requested expert bytes. Test actual GGUF offsets on supported filesystems and make any buffered fallback explicit and measured.

findings.title: Routing profiles can alias different checkpoints with the same tensor layout
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §6.2 keys a routing profile by a hash of each shard’s “tensor-info table and expert offsets,” rather than the shard contents or adapter weights.
findings.failure_scenario: A fine-tune, merged checkpoint, or other model has the same tensor names, shapes, types, and offsets but different router weights. It reuses the old profile and warm-fills experts that may no longer be hot, reducing early and held-out hit rates until local learning corrects it.
findings.why_it_matters: The profile is explicitly shareable and is used to choose initial residency; matching geometry is not evidence that routing frequencies transfer between weight contents.
findings.fix: Bind profiles to verified full-shard content hashes or a trusted model-release manifest, and include adapters or other routing-affecting files in the identity. Keep geometry validation as a separate safety check.

findings.title: The default for non-bitwise speculation conflicts with exact-by-default
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.1 defines exact mode as bitwise identity; §3.5 labels speculation class D as “not bitwise”; §8 leaves its default as “Chris decides”; and §12.2 repeats that decision as open.
findings.failure_scenario: If the eventual launcher enables n-gram or MTP speculation by default, a user can receive a path that the design itself says is not bitwise, despite the exact-by-default requirement. Distribution-preserving rejection sampling does not guarantee identical seeded tokens or logits.
findings.why_it_matters: The design cannot claim an exact default while leaving an explicitly non-bitwise mechanism’s default unresolved.
findings.fix: Set class D off in the exact profile by default. Expose it only through an explicitly named non-bitwise/verified-speculation mode, with the distinction visible in the plan and logs.

findings.title: The claimed machine generality is validated only with synthetic capacity caps
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §2 says the 8 GB case is a “ballast allocation on this GPU until a real 8 GB machine is available.” §10 M1.3 calls for an 8 GB / 16 GB-RAM simulation, while the reference system is a Windows RTX 4090 Laptop.
findings.failure_scenario: A same-GPU ballast or RAM cap does not reproduce a different GPU’s kernel eligibility, PCIe 3.0 transfer behavior, Linux pin limits/direct-I/O rules, or a slower NVMe device. A plan that passes the simulation may still miss its hit-rate or throughput targets, or fail its I/O path, on those machines.
findings.why_it_matters: The brief includes unlike machines and another quant layout in scope, while the design describes self-calibration as machine-general.
findings.fix: Define a bounded support matrix and validate at least one real low-VRAM/PCIe 3.0 system, one Linux system, a constrained-RAM/slower-NVMe system, and multiple expert layouts. Until then, describe these cases as unvalidated rather than self-calibrated.

findings.title: PERF: Benchmark an 8-row verify window before imposing a 7-row cap
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.3 says 8 rows sends IQ2_S to MMQ, which it lists as supporting IQ2_S; the IQ1_M fallback occurs at 9 rows. §8 caps Swift speculation at “window <= 7 rows.”
findings.failure_scenario: If the cap means total verify rows, high-acceptance prompts cannot use a supported 8-row batch, potentially leaving a useful candidate token out of each verification window. The MMQ path may also be slower, so the gain is not assured.
findings.why_it_matters: An 8-row measurement can test whether one more verified row amortizes fixed per-window work. Estimate: 0–10% decode improvement on favorable high-acceptance workloads, with no gain or a regression if MMQ is slower. This is class D, not bitwise exact; keep it opt-in. The cap belongs in the layer on top, with kernel-path validation in llama.cpp.
findings.fix: Specify whether the cap counts drafted tokens or total verify rows, then benchmark 7 versus 8 total rows by milliseconds per committed token on each layout. Retain the lower cap if the 8-row path loses.

findings.title: PERF: Batch bank-fill submissions when misses fragment into many transfers
findings.evidence: The current fill loop can issue a separate `ggml_backend_tensor_set_async` for each role/range (`llama-moe-cache.cpp:593-605`). DESIGN-M1.md §5 P3/P5 adds a source interface and copy stream but does not specify batching those submissions. RESEARCH-PACK.md §5 reports that CUDA-13 DMA batching reduced host submission time, but total transfer time changed only from 2.5589 to 2.5248 ms; the reference toolchain is CUDA 12.8.
findings.failure_scenario: When SLRU victims make many noncontiguous fills, host submission overhead can remain on the critical path even after pinned staging and a copy stream are added.
findings.why_it_matters: A byte-preserving packed staging batch followed by a device scatter could reduce submission overhead. Estimate: 0–5% decode on a submission-bound workload, near zero when PCIe bandwidth dominates; this is an exact optimization and would live in the llama.cpp fill path/P3 source layer.
findings.fix: Count fill calls and host submission time first. If material, pack role slices into an aligned staging batch and transfer in fewer operations, then scatter unchanged bytes into the existing banks. Benchmark on CUDA 12.8 rather than relying on the CUDA-13 batching result.

brief_challenges.challenge: Define the 85% hit-rate target with a matched denominator and workload. The brief compares stock’s arithmetic 33% GPU share with Strata’s measured 85.4% lookup figure, but its own context notes Strata used MTP, route-tail skip, and a CPU/GPU split.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: Lookup hits, byte-weighted hits, and hits per committed token can differ, and route-tail skipping or speculation can alter which requests are counted. Without a fixed exact-only workload and denominator, the target can be met while the intended transfer or latency improvement is not.

brief_challenges.challenge: Replace “self-calibrating to any machine” with an explicit supported-hardware and software matrix, plus a separate statement of what is merely best-effort.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: A probe cannot guarantee correctness or performance across every GPU, driver, OS, filesystem, PCIe link, memory limit, and quant layout. Finite validation and explicit unsupported/fallback behavior make the requirement testable.

done_well: The design correctly distinguishes Strata’s measured speed from an exact-mode comparison and labels unmeasured estimates as estimates.
It builds on upstream’s per-expert banks and keeps misses on the GPU in the exact path, rather than assuming CPU fallback is bitwise equivalent.
It makes parity testing an early gate and recognizes that bank shape, slot IDs, and `MUL_MAT_ID` row count can affect numerical dispatch.
It separates lookup hit rate from byte-weighted hits, tier coverage, exposed wait, and prefetch lateness instead of treating one aggregate hit number as a performance explanation.
It identifies host-memory pressure and WDDM VRAM budgeting as first-order failure modes and rejects silent CPU fallback in exact mode.
could_not_verify: No build or GPU benchmark on the pinned commit was available; the design states it has not run. Upstream SLRU hit rate, decode speed, sync cost, and the predicted performance gains remain unverified.
The proposed asynchronous event ordering, live bank resizing, and direct-I/O behavior cannot be validated without an implementation and Windows/Linux hardware tests.
Bitwise parity across the disclosed row-count/kernel paths and behavior on real 8 GB, 16 GB-RAM, PCIe 3.0, Linux, and alternative-quant systems remain unverified.

critiques.summary: The design makes good use of upstream's cache and is unusually explicit about unmeasured performance and numerical risks. Its largest operational gaps are that M1 promises live memory reclamation without an allocation/control mechanism, postpones its principal RAM-pressure mitigation until M2, and does not yet define telemetry sufficient to substantiate several calibration decisions. Benchmark cache-state control, profile invalidation, serving concurrency, and release rollback also need stronger contracts before a newcomer can safely rely on self-calibration. The supplied cache source supports these concerns; no runtime behavior was verified.

findings.title: The M1 governor cannot reclaim VRAM merely by reducing the number of usable slots
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §7.7 promises to 'shrink the adaptive region by whole slots' under competing allocations, and §10 makes this an M1.3 exit test. In llama-moe-cache.cpp:388-453, bank tensors and their views are constructed at fixed dimensions and allocated through a single device context buffer. The supplied public wrappers expose no resize operation. DESIGN-M1.md §5 includes allocation lending only in P7, scheduled for M5.
findings.failure_scenario: Another application consumes VRAM. Marian invalidates adaptive slots or lowers a policy limit, but the underlying device allocation remains unchanged. Alternatively, rebuilding the bank temporarily requires old and new allocations simultaneously, triggering the very OOM or WDDM spill the governor should prevent.
findings.why_it_matters: This leaves the M1.3 competing-allocation acceptance criterion unsupported by the planned patch set. Pausing admission does not release memory already allocated, and a Python launcher cannot safely mutate the child process's bank without an explicit control interface.
findings.fix: Add an M1 allocation-reclamation design and native control hook. Specify physically reclaimable allocation units, graph/view invalidation, reader draining, minimum transient capacity, and a shrink sequence that does not require a second full bank. If that exceeds M1 scope, document bounded request rejection and controlled restart into a smaller qualified plan instead of promising live shrink. Test actual driver-budget recovery, not just lower logical occupancy.

findings.title: M1's low-memory reliability depends on a byte-source fix deferred until M2
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §4 identifies pageable mmap uploads and post-prefill faults as the likely collapse mechanism. Section 11 labels RAM limitation 'high on Swift' and mitigates it with a RAM tier and unbuffered tail. However, §5 P3 and §10 defer both to M2, while M1.3 must work under a 16 GB RAM cap and M1 must reach 12 tok/s. The actual fill source remains w->data in llama-moe-cache.cpp:591-605. RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 records 10.59 versus 4.86 tok/s after two pp4096 passes, with page-cache state identified as a plausible cause rather than proven attribution.
findings.failure_scenario: Calibration selects an apparently successful warm plan. A long prompt subsequently displaces useful expert pages; decode then spends most of its time faulting host weights even though VRAM hit rate remains near the target. A smaller VRAM bank does not necessarily help and can increase host demand.
findings.why_it_matters: The design's own principal explanation for unstable laptop performance has no M1 mitigation. A brief fresh-process confirmation is insufficient evidence that a plan remains usable after ordinary serving workloads.
findings.fix: Make cold-start and pp4096/16K-to-decode endurance tests mandatory before M1 exit. Promote a minimal bounded source/staging implementation into M1 if these fail, or explicitly restrict M1 support to measured memory/workload envelopes and refuse unsupported plans. Record a disk-demand feasibility bound alongside the predicted hit rate.

findings.title: P1 does not yet specify how to measure actual readiness or per-token hits across all execution paths
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P1 instruments cache copy() and promises 'microseconds from ids-ready to bank-ready'; §9.2 uses this ring for per-token hit rate and exposed wait. In llama-moe-cache.cpp:583-605, the callback first synchronizes and then issues asynchronous uploads; callback elapsed time is not a completion timestamp. Its plan() counts hits over deduplicated uniq IDs at :114-137. get_slot_map() bypasses this path above 32 tokens or insufficient capacity at :496-505, and copy_experts() reports role-level copied ranges at :514-547.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation wraps copy() with a host timer and exports n_hit as token hits. It undercounts transfer completion time, mixes synchronization waiting for preceding work with avoidable drain overhead, and miscounts repeated expert selections in batched decode. Large prefill and bypass traffic are absent from the same trace.
findings.why_it_matters: These measurements decide whether to build P5, which policy wins replay, and whether M1 passes. Correct-looking statistics could therefore produce a wrong optimization decision or a false per-token hit-rate claim.
findings.fix: Specify separate timestamps for routing completion, host planning, upload submission, upload completion, and consumer readiness, with a documented critical-path interpretation. Capture a pre-admission residency mask for every selected row and retain request/token/ubatch identifiers. Instrument selective-copy and bypass paths too. Add trace-loss counters and invalidate acceptance runs with incomplete records. Test counters against synthetic repeated-ID batches and explicitly forced path transitions.

findings.title: Fresh processes and identical warm-up do not establish identical page-cache history
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §9.3.2 says fresh processes and the same discarded warm-up mean 'both arms see the same page-cache history.' RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 documents approximately twofold stock decode variation associated with prior prefill runs and reports very low available RAM. Section 9.3 specifies only two initial A-A runs to establish the day's noise floor.
findings.failure_scenario: Arm A faults model pages that remain available to B, while B's different residency policy or prefill access pattern changes the cache inherited by the next A. ABBA reduces simple time drift but does not eliminate policy-dependent cache carryover. Two A-A samples fail to reveal that asymmetry.
findings.why_it_matters: On this machine, the uncontrolled state is large enough to dominate the anticipated optimization gain and even the 12 tok/s acceptance threshold.
findings.fix: Define separate cold, controlled-warm, and post-prefill workloads. For each, document a reproducible cache-state preparation method, verify it with physical reads and memory measurements, and report when equivalent state cannot be established. Randomize or counterbalance arm order across independent rounds, freeze learned-profile inputs during comparisons, and collect repeated A-A observations throughout the experiment rather than treating one pair as a stable noise bound.

findings.title: Profile identity and invalidation omit changes that materially alter routing and service costs
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §6.2 keys routing profiles by a hash of tensor-info tables and expert offsets, not tensor payloads. Its machine profile invalidation names driver, GPU, RAM and power changes. Section 7.9 adds context and routing drift but not engine/build, adapter, KV representation, or model-drive changes. By contrast, ideas/astra-ideas.md 'Self-calibration and adaptation' calls for verified full-shard identity and remeasurement after engine, adapter, KV-setting, thermal, and storage-device changes.
findings.failure_scenario: A same-shape fine-tune replaces the model without changing tensor directories, or the model moves from fast NVMe to a slower drive. Marian reuses a profile that looks compatible but predicts the wrong experts or disk service cost. A fortnightly rebase similarly reuses timings despite changed kernels or workspace demand.
findings.why_it_matters: This undermines machine-independent calibration and makes performance regressions difficult for a newcomer to diagnose. Structural hashes are useful layout identities, but are not model-content identities.
findings.fix: Separate layout identity from verified model-content identity. Bind routing observations to full-shard hashes or a verified manifest, adapter identity and relevant numerical settings. Bind timing plans to engine/build, backend, context/KV configuration, and storage-device identity. Define schema versions, targeted invalidation, and an explicit command that explains why a profile was reused or rejected.

findings.title: Automatic cliff-finding and pinning probes lack a safe execution envelope
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §6.1 proposes allocating VRAM in 256 MiB steps until bandwidth collapses more than threefold, and pinning RAM in 1 GiB steps until available memory falls below a floor. Section 7.1 presents this as an approximately 90-second first-start probe. No probe-specific timeout, commit-limit stop rule, cancellation contract, Linux OOM handling, or recovery sequence is specified.
findings.failure_scenario: A newcomer starts calibration on a working laptop. The probe intentionally crosses a driver-memory cliff or consumes scarce physical RAM, causing desktop stalls, pagefile churn, allocation failures, or Linux OOM intervention. Measuring collapse can also perturb the state used by subsequent measurements.
findings.why_it_matters: Self-calibration should not require users to discover resource limits by destabilizing their active desktop. Small-memory machines are particularly exposed, and their first-use experience may fail before the model loads.
findings.fix: Use conservative reported-budget bounds for normal automatic probing and make destructive boundary exploration explicit opt-in. Run probes in a supervised subprocess with deadlines, cancellation and guaranteed cleanup; enforce both physical and commit/cgroup limits. Provide platform-specific allocation-failure handling and a conservative fallback plan. Require a recovery interval and resource-state check before further benchmarks.

findings.title: Fortnightly rebases and exit-time learning have no operational rollback or crash-safe persistence contract
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 schedules fortnightly master rebases and one commit per patch. Section 6.1 says serve merges learned counts at exit; §5 P4 dumps them on exit. The supplied design does not specify profile migrations, atomic publication, concurrent-writer handling, last-known-good plans, or binary/profile rollback. RESEARCH-PACK.md §5 explicitly notes Strata's temporary-file-and-rename writer, but this safeguard is not carried into the design.
findings.failure_scenario: An OOM or driver reset prevents exit-time learning from being saved. Two local server processes overwrite one another's profiles. After a rebase, a new binary updates a profile that the previous binary cannot read, so reverting the executable no longer restores a known-good serving setup.
findings.why_it_matters: The design depends on persistent learning and frequent upstream updates. Without a release and persistence contract, failures can create repeated cold starts, silent tuning loss, or a rollback that does not actually recover service.
findings.fix: Version profiles and plans, use atomic writes with checksums and writer coordination, and periodically checkpoint bounded learning increments. Keep immutable run manifests and a last-known-good binary/plan/profile bundle. Document upgrade qualification, downgrade behavior, how to disable individual patches, how to reset calibration safely, and how to collect diagnostic artifacts without sharing routing data by default.

findings.title: The serving contract does not constrain concurrency or define memory-pressure admission behavior
findings.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.1 conditions exactness on identical rows per MUL_MAT_ID call; §6.1 launches llama-server; §7.7 says to 'pause admission' under memory pressure. Sections 9 and 10 test prompts and an agent session but do not define server parallelism, continuous-batching settings, concurrent request tests, queue limits, or refusal behavior. llama-moe-cache.cpp:496-505 changes execution path with total n_tokens and capacity.
findings.failure_scenario: A second local client submits work while the first is decoding. The server combines rows, crosses a bank-capacity or kernel boundary, and consumes a different workspace peak than the calibrated single-request plan. The user has no documented way to tell whether a paused request is queued safely, stalled indefinitely, or must be retried.
findings.why_it_matters: Loopback binding does not imply one client or one request. Concurrency changes precisely the batch geometry on which the exactness and memory contracts depend, and can invalidate single-session capacity measurements.
findings.fix: For M1, explicitly enforce and document a qualified server concurrency/continuous-batching configuration, preferably one active sequence initially. Define bounded queuing, cancellation, timeout and refusal semantics using upstream server facilities. If concurrent serving is supported, calibrate aggregate batch geometry and workspace peaks, record realized row schedules, and add parity and competing-allocation tests under concurrent requests.

findings.title: PERF: Preserve upload coalescing when introducing ranked victims and transient slots
findings.evidence: llama-moe-cache.cpp:138-151 sorts missing expert IDs but selects each victim by SLRU traversal; :595-605 merges uploads only when both source expert IDs and destination slot IDs are consecutive. DESIGN-M1.md §5 P2 replaces victim selection and adds three slot classes without specifying transfer-run preservation. RESEARCH-PACK.md's byte addendum gives about 660 MiB of selected weights per token; at approximately 85% hits, roughly 72 expert misses remain.
findings.failure_scenario: Ranked admission improves hit rate but scatters misses across destination slots. With three roles, about 72 misses can require up to 216 separate upload submissions per token, losing coalescing that the current implementation sometimes obtains.
findings.why_it_matters: Avoidable submission overhead is material on a host-round-trip-heavy Windows path. A policy evaluated only for hit rate or transferred bytes can miss this regression.
findings.fix: In the llama.cpp policy patch, prefer contiguous free/transient destination runs for contiguous source misses, and use adjacency as a tie-break among otherwise equivalent eligible victims. Do not evict valuable residents solely to create runs. Extend replay and telemetry with upload-run counts. This is an exact candidate because it changes only placement and transfer grouping; gate it with slot-permutation parity. Illustrative gain: eliminating 100 submissions at a measured 5 microseconds each saves 0.5 ms/token, approximately 0.6% at 12 tok/s or 1.8% at 35.5 tok/s. Expect zero benefit where source IDs are scattered or submission is already hidden; measure before enabling.

brief_challenges.challenge: The headline target combines unlike hit-rate definitions: stock's arithmetic layer share, Strata's aggregate lookup fraction under approximate/speculative execution, and Marian's median per-token exact-mode hit rate.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: These are useful reference points but not equivalent measurements. An 85% target should specify workload, byte budget, warm-up state, batching and denominator independently of Strata's reported number.

brief_challenges.challenge: An 8 GB VRAM ballast and 16 GB RAM cap validate constrained capacity, not the performance or failure behavior of a real smaller laptop.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: They do not reproduce a narrower PCIe link, different memory bandwidth, shared-memory iGPU behavior, slower NVMe, Linux allocation failure, or thermal limits. Results should be labeled capacity simulation rather than validation of an entire machine class.

brief_challenges.challenge: The brief asks whether a newcomer can deploy, monitor and roll back safely, but supplies a design proposal rather than a release/runbook specification.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: Operational readiness needs explicit deliverables: supported configuration matrix, launch and verification commands, health/error semantics, diagnostic collection, upgrade qualification and rollback. Without these, feature completion can be mistaken for safe deployment.

brief_challenges.challenge: The reference laptop cannot provide the full all-experts-resident Swift oracle required by the stated exactness contract.
brief_challenges.why_it_matters: Single-layer tests and selective-copy comparisons are valuable, but the brief should identify who supplies a repeatable full-model reference or explicitly delimit what those substitute tests establish. This is a validation-resource gap, not an argument to weaken exact mode.

done_well: Clearly separates measured historical results, source facts, arithmetic estimates and untested proposals.
Uses upstream's existing bank storage and selective-copy mechanisms rather than introducing a second inference engine.
Makes exactness falsifiable with forced misses, slot permutations and eviction/reuse tests, and recognizes that identical weight bytes alone are insufficient.
Treats exposed stalls and RAM/NVMe coverage as more informative than VRAM hit rate alone.
Includes held-out reporting, an instrumentation-off control, explicit NO DECISION outcomes and early upstream-baseline falsifiers.
Keeps routing-profile sharing explicit and treats shared statistics as untrusted priors rather than executable configuration.
could_not_verify: No builds, GPU measurements, fault-injection tests or end-to-end exactness runs were performed.

Direct source inspection was limited to the supplied llama-moe-cache.cpp. Assertions about CUDA dispatch, scheduler behavior, loader laziness and the existing M0 adapter were assessed from the supplied design/research excerpts, not independently opened source files.
The supplied material does not establish actual server concurrency defaults, the eventual native control API, or how physical bank resizing would be implemented.
No deployment runbook, profile schema, trace schema, release manifest or implemented rollback procedure was supplied.
The coalescing improvement's gain depends on actual miss-ID locality and measured submission overhead; its numerical example is a sensitivity estimate, not a benchmark.

items.title: Bind expert sidecars to payload bytes, not just tensor metadata
items.verdict_reason: The design specifies a metadata-and-offset hash for routing profiles but does not specify the sidecar's identity check. Reusing that hash for expert bytes would break exactness; the text does not establish that it will be reused.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§4, 5 P3, 6.2 proposes a derived expert source but specifies only a tensor-info/offset hash. The current fill reads the original tensor at llama-moe-cache.cpp:591-605.
items.failure_scenario: A replacement GGUF retains tensor geometry and offsets but changes expert payloads; an old sidecar supplies the wrong weights.
items.why_it_matters: Wrong expert bytes silently violate the bitwise exactness contract.
items.fix: Specify a separate verified payload identity for every source shard and sidecar record, or a trusted payload-hash manifest. Publish sidecars atomically and reject mismatches.

items.title: The M1 governor cannot physically shrink upstream's fixed bank
items.severities: S-02: High; L-02: High; A-01: High
items.verdict_reason: Shrinking logical residency or pausing admission does not release the bank allocation. No M1 patch or control interface provides physical resizing.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §7.7 promises whole-slot shrinkage and §10 tests competing allocations at M1.3. Bank dimensions and buffers are fixed at construction in llama-moe-cache.cpp:304-365, 388-470; P7 lending is deferred to M5.
items.failure_scenario: Another process consumes VRAM; Marian invalidates slots, but its allocated bytes remain and WDDM spill or OOM persists.
items.why_it_matters: The stated M1.3 memory-pressure exit test is unsupported, on hardware with a documented several-fold cliff.
items.fix: Implement reclaimable bank segments with safe graph rebinding and reader draining, or specify a controlled stop/restart into a smaller qualified plan. Test driver-budget recovery, not slot occupancy.

items.title: PERF: Put a minimal bounded expert source before the M1 throughput exit
items.verdict_reason: The scheduling gap is real, but neither paging causality nor failure of the 12 tok/s floor has been measured on the new pin.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§10-11 puts P3's RAM/staging/NVMe path in M2 despite the M1 decode floor. Until then fills use w->data (llama-moe-cache.cpp:591-605). RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 reports approximately 19 GiB initially free RAM, a roughly 23.86 GiB non-VRAM expert complement at Strata-sized residency, and an older-build post-prefill slowdown.
items.failure_scenario: The policy reaches 85% VRAM hits, while remaining misses fault from mmap after a long prefill. At 85% byte hits, roughly 99 MiB/token remains; serving all of it at an illustrative 2 GiB/s would take about 48 ms/token before other work.
items.why_it_matters: A hit-rate pass need not yield the required sustained decode speed.
items.fix: Require cold and pp4096/16K-to-decode endurance tests at M1 exit. If they fail, advance bounded RAM, pinned staging and queued tail reads for both copy paths into M1. This is byte-preserving; estimated gain is zero without paging, potentially recovery of an approximately twofold paging-related slowdown.

items.title: P5b has no specified intra-token host service for a cold tail miss
items.verdict_reason: As specified, the miss ring is drained for admission between tokens, whereas a cold expert needs host I/O before the waiting layer can finish. A distinct timely demand-publication protocol is absent.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P5b specifies GPU-side resolve, a mapped-flag tail wait and between-token admission from a device miss ring; §7 expects an NVMe tail on smaller machines.
items.failure_scenario: The GPU waits for an NVMe-backed expert whose ID is not delivered to a host reader until the token completes.
items.why_it_matters: A bounded wait avoids a long GPU hang but neither supplies the expert nor preserves exact execution.
items.fix: Use P5a for cold tails initially. For P5b, define intra-token demand publication, a concurrent reader, system-scope data/flag ordering, error propagation and an exact timeout fallback; force cold misses and I/O errors in tests.

items.title: The proposed cache callback misses large-batch prefill routing
items.verdict_reason: P1's specified copy() hook runs only for the small-cache slot-map path. The design mentions an eval callback before P1, but does not carry equivalent large-batch tracing into P1/P4.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P1 places selected-ID tracing in llama-moe-cache.cpp:549-617 and P4's phase counts in the cache. get_slot_map() bypasses that path above 32 tokens or insufficient capacity at :496-507; copy_experts() at :514-547 reports resident ranges, not all selected rows. RESEARCH-PACK.md §3 describes the separate selective-copy callback.
items.failure_scenario: A 20k-token calibration corpus uses large prefill ubatches; its persisted prefill counts omit or bias most prefill selections.
items.why_it_matters: Replay accuracy and phase-specific plans could be certified against an incomplete trace.
items.fix: Trace at a shared routing point or instrument the large-batch selective-copy path too. Retain token/row and phase identity, and require expected selection counts for pp4096 before accepting a profile.

items.title: Distinct-expert cache counters are not row-level lookup hits
items.verdict_reason: Upstream de-duplicates selected IDs before counting hits and fills. This chiefly affects multirow batches; single-token top-k selections do not have the same duplicate problem.
items.evidence: llama-moe-cache.cpp:109-152 constructs uniq and increments n_hit once per distinct resident expert; :608-611 adds n_hit and fills.size() to aggregate stats. DESIGN-M1.md §9.2 instead defines per-token hits over 480 routed selections.
items.failure_scenario: Two verify rows select the same resident expert: upstream counts one hit, but a row-level metric counts two.
items.why_it_matters: Reusing upstream counters can misstate batched hit rate and replay accuracy. Marian's median per-token figure also cannot be equated directly with Strata's reported aggregate.
items.fix: Record pre-admission residency for every selected row, alongside distinct fills and copied bytes. Report per-token distributions and aggregate lookup fractions separately.

items.title: P1 does not define a valid bank-ready or exposed-wait timestamp
items.verdict_reason: The promised timing starts after a broad synchronization but the callback only submits asynchronous fills. Its elapsed host time is neither upload completion nor necessarily avoidable synchronization cost.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P1 promises time from IDs-ready to bank-ready and §9.2 exposed wait. llama-moe-cache.cpp:582-584 synchronizes before planning; :591-605 submits asynchronous bank writes; :611-614 submits the slot-map write and says a subsequent copy synchronizes.
items.failure_scenario: A callback timer attributes preceding GPU work to cache overhead and excludes outstanding uploads, leading to an incorrect P5 decision.
items.why_it_matters: These timings govern both performance claims and which optimization the design builds.
items.fix: Define routing-complete, planning, submission, transfer-complete and consumer-ready events, plus a critical-path calculation. Capture trace-loss counts and invalidate incomplete measurements.

items.title: A coarse standalone VRAM probe cannot certify the serving budget
items.verdict_reason: The risk is consistent with the plan, but §7.5 does include a short live finalist confirmation. The older baseline's 16,018 and 16,040 MiB peaks came from different configurations; their 22 MiB difference does not measure an exact spill threshold.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§6.1, 7.1-7.5 specifies 256 MiB probe steps, a greater-than-3× collapse trigger, subtractive sizing and one short live confirmation. RESEARCH-PACK.md §§1, 10 reports a sharp observed performance change and no validated 16K serving budget.
items.failure_scenario: A small model-free operation stays fast at a proposed allocation, while server workspace, growing KV or another process causes spill during a full request.
items.why_it_matters: The result could be several-fold throughput loss without an allocation error.
items.fix: Use the standalone probe as a bound, then validate the loaded model at requested context and peak ubatch, refine steps near the boundary, treat allocation failures as signals and record headroom throughout competing-load tests.

items.title: The Swift parity gate lacks its literal same-GPU all-resident oracle
items.verdict_reason: The design acknowledges that Swift cannot fit and substitutes valuable but non-identical tests. Those tests do not directly establish its stated whole-Swift, same-GPU reference.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.1 defines that reference; §3.6 substitutes E0 single layers, E2 another model and E2b Swift cache/selective-copy comparisons. RESEARCH-PACK.md's byte addendum puts Swift routed experts alone at 33.02 GiB versus 16 GB VRAM.
items.failure_scenario: All surrogate tests pass while an unexercised Swift graph shape or bank-dependent dispatch differs from an all-resident Swift execution.
items.why_it_matters: E0-E2b should not be presented as proof of the literal whole-model contract.
items.fix: State and test a per-operation equivalence obligation across Swift shapes, documenting its compositional assumption. Where available, add a whole-Swift comparison on a sufficiently large, appropriately matched GPU without calling it the laptop's same-GPU oracle.

items.title: A cache-off Swift comparison may not isolate an upstream cache exactness defect
items.severities: Added by verifier; no critic severity
items.verdict_reason: The design calls cache on/off a preliminary upstream exactness check, but the supplied research explicitly says host-resident weights can lead either to host computation or to selective GPU copying. It does not establish which path this particular cache-off run takes.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.6 E2b says both compared Swift paths compute on GPU and that cache-on/off disagreement finds an upstream exactness problem. RESEARCH-PACK.md §2 distinguishes CPU execution from GPU selective copying; llama-moe-cache.cpp:496-507 only establishes when the cache slot-map path is used.
items.failure_scenario: Cache-off selects CPU expert kernels, producing different last bits for an expected reason rather than demonstrating a defective GPU bank.
items.why_it_matters: The first parity gate could reject a correct cache or misdiagnose the fix.
items.fix: Record the backend and kernel of each compared expert operation. Compare GPU bank and GPU selective-copy paths at identical row geometry; label any CPU comparison as a separate numerical-path test.

items.title: PERF: Avoid making the entire ranked warm fill a first-token barrier
items.verdict_reason: The design requires pre-first-token filling but does not fix its eventual size or measure cold-start cost.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §4 fills the ranked core before the first token and §9.2 measures first-token time. RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 reports 9.16 GiB for Strata's expert residency, not a measured Marian warm-fill size.
items.failure_scenario: A short cold request waits for gigabytes of experts it never selects.
items.why_it_matters: Steady-state decode can improve while time to first token becomes much worse.
items.fix: In the llama.cpp P2 fill and Marian launch plan, test a small synchronous high-value core followed by demand-prioritized background fill with lease-safe publication. Exact placement-only change; at an illustrative 2 GiB/s, deferring 8 GiB could avoid about 4 seconds of startup I/O, with possibly zero steady-state gain.

items.title: P5a must order slot-map lookup, not just the bank matmul
items.verdict_reason: P5a is unimplemented, so a missing wait cannot be observed. Its written event scheme mentions a wait at the consuming bank operation but not at the earlier GET_ROWS lookup.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P5a says the bank op waits for copy completion. The existing map publication follows fills in llama-moe-cache.cpp:591-614; DESIGN-M1.md §3.4 and RESEARCH-PACK.md §3 place slot lookup before MUL_MAT_ID.
items.failure_scenario: GET_ROWS consumes an old slot map, then the matmul waits for newly filled, different contents of that slot.
items.why_it_matters: This can silently produce incorrect logits in a mechanism classified as exact.
items.fix: Gate GET_ROWS on publication of the correct map generation and gate bank consumption on matching fill completion. Use versioned maps and reader leases; stress delayed publication and reuse.

items.title: The parity gate does not enumerate the kernel row-count boundaries it identifies
items.verdict_reason: The design identifies 7-, 8- and 9-row behavior but does not require those shapes in E0-E2b. Its generated-token and teacher-forced tests do not guarantee that coverage.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.3 describes the MMVQ/MMQ/fallback boundaries; §3.6 lists E0-E2b without a row-count or prefill-ubatch matrix. llama-moe-cache.cpp:496-507 also changes paths at capacity and above 32 tokens.
items.failure_scenario: One-row parity passes, but a verify window or large-batch selective-copy operation diverges.
items.why_it_matters: A merge gate could certify fewer numerical paths than exact mode offers.
items.fix: Require representative 1, 7, 8, 9 and 32 rows, capacity-boundary cases, large-batch fallback and actual prefill ubatches for each Swift layout. Compare intermediate outputs and logits.

items.title: Unbuffered expert reads need an explicit alignment and fallback contract
items.verdict_reason: Direct-I/O alignment requirements are real, but no P3 reader exists yet; an implementation might add the omitted handling.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§4-5 P3 proposes FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING/O_DIRECT for GGUF ranges without defining aligned offsets, lengths and buffers. ideas/fable-ideas.md Idea 4 explicitly notes GGUF offsets can require sector rounding and trimming.
items.failure_scenario: A cold slice fails an unbuffered read, or an implicit buffered fallback restores page-cache churn.
items.why_it_matters: The proposed low-RAM tail must work across supported filesystems and operating systems.
items.fix: Discover platform alignment, round ranges outward into aligned bounce buffers and copy the requested bytes. Make buffered fallback explicit, bounded and measured; test actual shard offsets.

items.title: Routing and timing profiles omit content and configuration invalidation
items.verdict_reason: A tensor-directory hash does not identify router weights, and the listed machine re-probe triggers omit several changes that affect execution or storage service.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §6.2 keys routing to tensor-info tables and offsets; §§6.2, 7.9 list driver/GPU/RAM/power/context/drift triggers, not full model or adapter payload, engine build, KV setting or model-drive change.
items.failure_scenario: A same-layout fine-tune inherits the wrong hot-expert ranking, or a model move/rebase inherits obsolete disk or workspace timings.
items.why_it_matters: Warm-hit and machine-fitted performance predictions become unreliable without a visible identity mismatch.
items.fix: Separate layout identity from verified full-shard and adapter identity. Version timing plans by build/backend, KV and context settings, and storage device; expose why each profile was reused or invalidated.

items.title: The class-D default remains unresolved despite exact-by-default
items.verdict_reason: This is an unresolved design decision, not evidence that non-bitwise speculation is currently enabled. Nonetheless, one allowed outcome of the stated open decision contradicts the fixed exact-default requirement.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§3.1, 3.5 calls exact mode bitwise and class D not bitwise; §§8, 12.2 asks whether class D should be default.
items.failure_scenario: The launcher defaults to verified speculation and produces non-bitwise logits or a different seeded token sequence while advertising an exact default.
items.why_it_matters: Distribution-preserving sampling does not satisfy the specified bitwise contract.
items.fix: Make class D off in the exact default, with a visibly named non-bitwise mode if enabled. Keep its quality gate separate from exactness tests.

items.title: A ballast and RAM cap do not validate unlike machines
items.verdict_reason: The proposed M1.3 second class is a simulation on the reference GPU; it cannot exercise a different GPU, PCIe link, OS I/O implementation or filesystem.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§2, 10 specifies an 8 GB ballast and 16 GB RAM cap until real hardware is available, yet §7 describes calibration as working on any machine.
items.failure_scenario: A plan passes the capacity simulation but fails direct I/O, pinning, kernel eligibility or throughput on a Linux PCIe 3.0 laptop.
items.why_it_matters: Capacity validation would be mistaken for hardware and software generality.
items.fix: Label the ballast result a capacity simulation. Define a supported matrix, real low-VRAM and Linux/slow-link tests, alternative-layout parity, and an explicit degraded or unsupported outcome.

items.title: PERF: Measure eight total verification rows before capping at seven
items.verdict_reason: The proposed Swift cap is seven rows even though the design itself places the IQ1_M fallback at nine. Whether the eighth row pays despite IQ2_S switching to MMQ is unmeasured.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.3 describes the 8- and 9-row kernel changes; §8 says speculation window <= 7 rows.
items.failure_scenario: A high-acceptance request loses a useful verification row solely because of an unbenchmarked cap.
items.why_it_matters: There may be avoidable fixed work per committed token.
items.fix: Define the cap in total verify rows and benchmark seven versus eight by milliseconds and expert bytes per committed token. This layer-on-top change remains class D, not bitwise exact; estimated favorable-workload gain is 0-10%, including possible regression.

items.title: PERF: Preserve coalescing and measure fill-submission overhead
items.verdict_reason: The source confirms that coalescing requires consecutive source IDs and destination slots; whether P2 fragments them enough to matter, or batching helps on CUDA 12.8, needs measurement.
items.evidence: llama-moe-cache.cpp:138-151 sorts misses and selects victims; :591-605 merges only consecutive expert/slot runs. DESIGN-M1.md §5 P2 adds ranked and transient classes without a coalescing rule. RESEARCH-PACK.md §5 reports a CUDA-13 submission microbenchmark but no established full-engine gain.
items.failure_scenario: Roughly 72 misses/token at 85% lookup hits produce many small role-wise uploads after scattered victim assignment.
items.why_it_matters: A better hit curve can still lose exposed host time on a submission-bound path.
items.fix: In the llama.cpp P2/P3 path, track upload runs and submission time, prefer contiguous eligible slots without sacrificing valuable residents, and test packed staging plus unchanged-byte scatter if needed. Exact placement/transfer change; estimated 0-5% decode gain, near zero if bandwidth dominates.

items.title: Identical warm-up in fresh processes does not equalize page-cache history
items.verdict_reason: The stated implication is false: process exit does not reset OS cached pages, and arms with different access patterns can change the next arm's starting state.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §9.3.2 claims both arms see the same page-cache history after identical warm-up and fresh processes. RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 documents large older-build variation associated with memory pressure and prior prefill, without proving a single cause.
items.failure_scenario: A's reads warm or displace pages for B; an ABBA round then measures carryover rather than just the patch.
items.why_it_matters: Cache-state effects can exceed the claimed optimization and distort the 12 tok/s decision.
items.fix: Separate cold, controlled-warm and post-prefill arms; verify starting state with physical reads and available-memory metrics. Counterbalance order, freeze learning and repeat A-A checks through the experiment.

items.title: Automatic limit probes lack a safe resource envelope
items.verdict_reason: The design specifies deliberate VRAM-cliff exploration and 1 GiB pinning increments but no probe-specific timeout, cancellation, commit/cgroup bound or recovery procedure.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§6.1, 7.1 presents those tests as part of an approximately 90-second first-start probe.
items.failure_scenario: Calibration destabilizes an active desktop or exhausts memory before it has a usable plan.
items.why_it_matters: First-use failure is especially likely to affect the constrained laptops the design intends to support.
items.fix: Use conservative reported-budget limits automatically; make destructive boundary exploration opt-in. Supervise probes with deadlines, cleanup, physical/commit limits and a conservative fallback.

items.title: Learned profiles and fortnightly rebases lack crash-safe rollback rules
items.verdict_reason: Exit-time persistence and a rebase cadence are specified; atomic writes, concurrent writers, schema compatibility and a last-known-good bundle are not.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P4 and §6.1 write/merge counts at exit; §5's rebase policy updates fortnightly. RESEARCH-PACK.md §5 describes an atomic temporary-file-and-rename writer in prior art, not in Marian's plan.
items.failure_scenario: A crash loses a session's learning, or a new binary rewrites a profile that a rolled-back binary cannot read.
items.why_it_matters: Persistent calibration and rollback can fail together, causing repeated cold starts or hard-to-diagnose regressions.
items.fix: Version and atomically publish profiles, coordinate writers, checkpoint bounded increments and retain an immutable last-known-good binary/plan/profile bundle.

items.title: Serving concurrency and memory-pressure admission are undefined
items.verdict_reason: The design conditions parity on row geometry and promises to pause admission but specifies neither a qualified server concurrency setting nor queue, cancellation and refusal behavior.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §§3.1, 6.1, 7.7, 9-10; llama-moe-cache.cpp:496-507 changes cache path with token count and capacity.
items.failure_scenario: A second loopback client changes batch/workspace peaks or crosses a cache-path boundary; a paused client has no specified completion or retry outcome.
items.why_it_matters: A single-request calibration does not certify ordinary concurrent serving or its exactness comparisons.
items.fix: For M1, enforce one qualified active sequence or explicitly qualify concurrent schedules. Define bounded queuing, cancellation, timeout and refusal using upstream server facilities; test realized row schedules and peak allocations.

items.title: Protected-core policy needs an explicit transient-capacity invariant
items.severities: Added by verifier; no critic severity
items.verdict_reason: P2 has not been implemented. The text allows hysteretic core demotion but does not say when it must occur or reserve sufficient evictable slots for every eligible request.
items.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §4 defines a protected ranked core and transient slots. The upstream eligibility check compares the possible selected set with all group slots at llama-moe-cache.cpp:496-507; its planner must obtain a distinct usable slot for each selected expert at :109-152.
items.failure_scenario: A request passes the total-slot check but selects more nonresident experts than the adaptive and transient regions can serve while the core remains protected.
items.why_it_matters: An otherwise valid exact request could abort or require an unplanned numerical fallback, especially with small banks or verify windows.
items.fix: Specify a per-group evictable-capacity invariant for each supported row count, immediate safe core demotion when required, and selective-copy fallback before an impossible plan. Test all-core-cold selections.

collated.agreement: All three critics accept upstream's per-expert cache as a sensible starting point and agree that the proposed gains have not been measured on the pin. They independently identify the non-reclaiming M1 governor, the deferred RAM/NVMe repair, and gaps between proposed telemetry or validation and the conclusions drawn from them.
collated.notes: Verdicts assess the written design and supplied source, not an implementation. In particular, the older stock slowdown does not prove paging on the new pin, the reported 22 MiB difference between older VRAM peaks is not a measured cliff width, and Strata's aggregate hit result is not Marian's proposed median per-token metric.
