C-02.reason: The M1 governor promises physical relief it has no scheduled mechanism to provide. Upstream fixes bank dimensions and allocates the device buffer at construction; changing which slots the policy admits does not shrink that allocation. The design defers bank lending to M5. A controlled restart could address this, but is not specified.
C-02.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §7.7: “shrink the adaptive region by whole slots”; §10 makes avoiding collapse under a competing allocation an M1.3 exit test. P7 is scheduled for M5. llama-moe-cache.cpp constructs banks with `g.n_slots + 1` and allocates `d.buf` with `ggml_backend_alloc_ctx_tensors_from_buft`.

C-07.reason: P1 promises bank-ready and exposed-wait measurements without defining completion events or accounting across paths. The existing callback synchronizes to obtain IDs, then merely submits asynchronous fills; its return cannot serve as a bank-ready timestamp. Its existing hit counter also counts distinct IDs, not each selected row. This is a specification gap, not evidence that a future implementation must use an invalid host timer.
C-07.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P1 promises “microseconds from ids-ready to bank-ready,” and §9.2 uses exposed wait and per-token hits. llama-moe-cache.cpp calls `ggml_backend_synchronize(backend)` before `plan()`, later issues `ggml_backend_tensor_set_async` for fills and the slot map, and increments hits from `n_hit` over `uniq`. `get_slot_map()` bypasses that path for large or over-capacity batches.

C-12.reason: As written, P5a names a wait for the bank operation but not for the preceding slot lookup. Waiting only at the matmul cannot repair a slot ID already read from an old map. This is a conditional flaw in the proposed ordering, not an observed bug in an implemented P5a.
C-12.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §5 P5a says “the bank op waits on a copy-complete event.” RESEARCH-PACK.md §3 describes `GET_ROWS` of the host slot map before the bank’s `MUL_MAT_ID`. In the supplied cache source, `copy()` submits the updated slot-map copy after the expert fills.

C-13.reason: The merge-gating tests do not explicitly require the row-count and cache-path boundary cases the design identifies. That does not prove a parity failure; it means the stated gate may leave configurations untested. The original critic rated this Medium—the merged High label overstates the demonstrated consequence.
C-13.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.3 identifies different behavior at 7, 8 and 9 rows, but §3.6 specifies no corresponding E0–E2b row-count matrix. llama-moe-cache.cpp also bypasses its slot-map path when `n_tokens > max_batch` or the conservative selected-set bound exceeds `n_slots`.

C-16.reason: The design correctly labels class D as non-bitwise, but still leaves open whether it is enabled by default. Enabling it in the exact default would conflict with the brief’s bitwise requirement. No violation is shown to be occurring now; the original finding is the unresolved default, which the text confirms.
C-16.evidence: The brief requires exact mode to be bitwise identical to the all-VRAM reference. DESIGN-M1.md §3.5 calls speculation “D (distribution-preserving, not bitwise),” while §§8 and 12.2 leave its default to “Chris decides.”

C-17.reason: The proposed second-class test varies capacity on the reference machine, not its GPU, link, operating system or storage. The design explicitly calls this a simulation and does not pretend it is a real 8 GB laptop test; nevertheless, that simulation alone cannot validate its broad machine-general calibration claim. The original finding was Medium, rather than a demonstrated High-severity failure on another machine.
C-17.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §2 calls the 8 GB case “a ballast allocation on this GPU until a real 8 GB machine is available”; §10 specifies an “8 GB / 16 GB-RAM simulation.” Section 7 says the plan is “Never tuned for one machine.” The brief expressly includes Linux, PCIe 3.0, slower NVMe and another quant layout.

C-20.reason: Fresh processes and an identical warm-up do not establish identical starting OS page-cache state, especially when the compared arms can read different pages. ABBA ordering helps with drift but does not establish the stated equivalence. The observed older-build variation makes this a material measurement risk, without proving that page-cache carryover caused any particular result.
C-20.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §9.3.2 says fresh processes and the same discarded warm-up mean “both arms see the same page-cache history.” RESEARCH-PACK.md §1 reports decode ranging from 10.59 to 4.86 tok/s after prior prefill and explicitly describes page-cache state as a plausible, not controlled, contributor.

C-23.reason: The serving plan launches llama-server and proposes pausing admission, but specifies neither a qualified concurrency setting nor what happens to queued or paused requests. The exactness definition conditions comparison on equal rows, while concurrency can change those rows and the required workspace. This identifies an unsupported serving configuration, not proof that every concurrent execution breaks parity.
C-23.evidence: DESIGN-M1.md §3.1 requires “the same rows per `MUL_MAT_ID` call”; §6.1 launches `llama-server`; §7.7 says to “pause admission or refuse a request” under pressure. Sections 9–10 give no concurrency or queue contract. llama-moe-cache.cpp `get_slot_map()` selects a different path according to token count and slot capacity.

scores.time_comment: The remaining work is mainly to define what the design means by full identity binding: for example, a verified payload manifest or content hashes that bind each sidecar record to the source weights. Section 11 already requires full identity binding and record verification, so clarifying that requirement should take hours rather than require an architectural change.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This does not require a new inference kernel or broad coordination. The implementation would need sidecar-generation and load-time validation, with some cost for generating or checking hashes, but the design has already identified the required safeguard.
scores.quality_comment: A shape-compatible but stale sidecar could silently violate bitwise exactness, so specifying payload-level validation matters. The incremental gain is limited because the existing risk table already calls for identity binding and record verification; the finding overstates the omission if read as saying there is no guard at all.
scores.urgency_comment: The sidecar is optional and its source interface is deferred to M2. The failure would be serious if a mismatched sidecar were accepted, but the design already names the failure and required controls, so this is a low-immediacy clarification.

scores.time_comment: Invalidating slots cannot release the bank allocation: the source constructs banks with fixed dimensions and allocates their buffers at initialization. A genuinely dynamic shrink would need safe buffer segmentation, graph rebinding and reader draining; a less ambitious stop-and-restart into a smaller plan could be implemented sooner, but neither behavior is specified as the M1 governor response.
scores.cost_effort_comment: In-place resizing crosses cache policy, allocator, scheduler and in-flight GPU work, with corruption or OOM risk if a buffer is released too early. A restart-based fallback is cheaper but changes serving behavior and requires reliable request refusal and recovery; either path needs stress testing under WDDM pressure.
scores.quality_comment: Fixing this makes the promised response to competing VRAM allocations physically effective, rather than merely reducing logical residency while retaining the same VRAM footprint. That is important on the reference laptop given the reported sharp slowdown near the VRAM limit, although static conservative planning may still work when no other process takes memory.
scores.urgency_comment: The issue is directly in the M1.3 governor and its competing-allocation test, so it should be resolved before that milestone is treated as passing. Harm is conditional on memory pressure, but the design explicitly promises adaptation in that condition and the cost of an ineffective response could be a spill or OOM.

scores.time_comment: Advancing a bounded source into M1 means implementing more than a measurement: it needs a staging path, source selection, memory bounds, and consistent use by the small-cache fill and large-batch copier. A minimal pinned staging and bounded RAM path is plausibly a multi-week effort; a full sidecar and robust unbuffered NVMe tier is larger still.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This adds platform-specific memory and I/O management to a path currently reading `w->data`, and both upstream copy paths must remain correct. The benefit is uncertain on the new pin, so the appropriate cost includes the cold, post-prefill and constrained-memory tests needed before making it a default.
scores.quality_comment: This could be decisive for the 12 tok/s M1 floor if misses fault from storage: roughly 99 MiB per token at an assumed 85% byte hit rate would take about 48 ms at 2 GiB/s before other work. That calculation is illustrative, not a measured prediction: lookup hit rate is not byte hit rate, and the new pin has not been tested. The fix is therefore valuable but conditional on the proposed endurance measurements.
scores.urgency_comment: P3 is deferred to M2 even though M1 has a sustained decode target and the supplied older-build results show serious host-memory pressure and a post-prefill slowdown. M1.0 can first establish whether this threatens the new build; if it does, deferring the source path would put the M1 exit at risk.

scores.time_comment: A usable P5b needs a way for the host to learn about a cold expert request and complete its NVMe read while the current token is waiting, plus ordering and error handling for publication of the bytes. Defining and validating that protocol is likely a multi-week CUDA, I/O and concurrency task; choosing P5a for cold misses would be a faster safe alternative.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This is a high-risk cross-device protocol involving a GPU miss ring, mapped host memory, asynchronous file reads, memory visibility, timeouts and exact failure behavior. It also needs tests for cold misses, I/O errors, delayed publication and slot reuse, not just a successful warm-RAM case.
scores.quality_comment: If P5b is implemented as written, a cold tail miss can wait for a host service that only drains the miss ring between tokens. The GPU may time out or the token may never get the required bytes; either outcome defeats the exact miss-computation contract. A demand-publication path or a P5a fallback would remove a serious correctness and liveness risk.
scores.urgency_comment: This is a real defect in the P5b alternative, but P5 is scheduled for M2 and the design offers P5a as another candidate. It is not an immediate M1 blocker if cold-tail service is kept off the critical path until the protocol is complete.

scores.time_comment: Tracing large-batch routing can be added at a shared routing point or in the selective-copy path, and phase labels can be retained in the profile. The work is a few days if the existing eval callback can provide reliable IDs for the full calibration run; it is longer if both graph paths need new instrumentation.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The change is localized to routing telemetry and profile construction rather than the numerical kernels. It still needs coverage checks for prefill batches that bypass `get_slot_map`, and coordination with the P3 source interface if that copier is also being changed.
scores.quality_comment: The cache `copy()` path is not a complete source of prefill observations: `get_slot_map()` can bypass it above 32 tokens or when capacity is insufficient, while `copy_experts()` sees resident copies rather than every routed row. However, the design explicitly says the existing eval callback can record `ffn_moe_topk` IDs before P1, so the finding is partly mitigated. Ensure that this alternative also supplies P4's phase-specific learning and validate counts on a large prefill.
scores.urgency_comment: M1.1 builds routing profiles from mixed workloads, so an incomplete prefill trace could distort prefill statistics and replay conclusions soon. It is less urgent for the stated held-out decode hit-rate target, which is measured separately, and the pre-P1 eval callback offers a path around the omission.

scores.time_comment: No correction is needed to the design as stated: it defines the decode metric as hits over 480 routed lookups and requires a per-token trace of selected IDs. The implementation should count pre-admission residency per row rather than copy upstream's distinct-expert aggregate, but that is a straightforward implementation check.
scores.cost_effort_comment: A row-level counter can be derived from the IDs and residency map already needed by P1, before `plan()` mutates that map. This adds little code or coordination; no separate cache-policy redesign is required.
scores.quality_comment: The upstream `n_hit` count is indeed per distinct expert, not per selected row, so it must not be reported as the design's 480-lookup denominator for multirow batches. But the design does not specify reusing that counter, and its explicit denominator and ID-trace requirement point to the correct metric. The alleged measurement defect is not established.
scores.urgency_comment: There is no current defect to fix in the written measurement definition. During implementation, a synthetic duplicate-ID test would cheaply ensure that row-level and distinct-expert counts remain separate.

scores.time_comment: The instrumentation needs distinct timestamps for routing completion, host planning, upload submission, slot-map publication, transfer completion and the consumer's actual readiness. Adding those events and a critical-path calculation is a several-day task, especially because host callback time alone cannot express GPU completion.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The change is principally instrumentation and event plumbing, but it must avoid adding synchronization that changes the behavior being measured. It also needs trace-loss reporting and an instrumentation-off comparison to validate overhead.
scores.quality_comment: The source synchronizes after requesting IDs, then submits expert and slot-map writes asynchronously. Timing the whole callback can include preceding GPU work and omit outstanding uploads, so it may misstate both drain cost and bank-ready time. Those measurements drive the M1.0 decision about P5; invalid timing could send effort toward the wrong bottleneck.
scores.urgency_comment: M1.0 explicitly uses drain timing to re-scope P5, and P1 makes exposed-wait measurements central to later decisions. This should be specified before the first measurements, even though it does not itself change model outputs.

scores.time_comment: The practical fix is to make live validation explicitly cover the requested context, peak prefill ubatch and a controlled competing allocation, then refine the budget near the observed boundary. The design already has a live finalist confirmation and context-aware budgeting, so the remaining work is better qualification rather than replacing the probe.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This mainly adds a few loaded-server calibration runs and clearer acceptance rules. It is a manageable addition, although it may take longer on machines where full-context runs or competing-load tests are slow.
scores.quality_comment: A small model-free allocation and matmul can identify a useful bound but cannot alone reproduce server workspace, context-dependent KV and competing allocations. The design does not rely solely on that probe: it also calculates context costs, confirms finalists live, measures 16K prefill and tests under competition. The finding remains partly valid because those checks are not explicitly required to reach the worst-case serving boundary.
scores.urgency_comment: The budget finder is part of M1.3, but the written plan already includes more than the standalone probe and the old 22 MiB comparison is not a measured spill threshold. The risk matters before general release, but is not as immediate as the missing event semantics or exactness coverage.

scores.time_comment: The tests need an explicit statement of how E0 layer-level parity, E2b Swift path comparisons and row-shape coverage compose into a whole-model exactness argument. Obtaining a literal all-resident Swift reference would require a suitably large matched GPU and may not be possible on the reference laptop; documenting and testing the compositional alternative is the more practical near-term fix.
scores.cost_effort_comment: A defensible argument must cover every numerical path and relevant shape, not merely add a single end-to-end run. A larger-GPU test adds hardware and configuration coordination, while a compositional test matrix adds engineering and review effort.
scores.quality_comment: The design correctly recognizes that 33.02 GiB of routed experts cannot fit in the reference 16 GB GPU and substitutes useful single-layer and selective-copy checks. Those tests can support an exactness claim if their assumptions are stated and the row, layout and graph interactions are covered. As written, E0-E2b should not be presented as a literal same-GPU whole-Swift comparison.
scores.urgency_comment: This is important before declaring E0-E2b a proof of the exactness contract, but the design already acknowledges the missing all-resident Swift reference and has surrogate gates. The issue is a qualification and coverage gap to close during M1, not evidence that the cache currently produces wrong answers.

scores.time_comment: Record the backend and row geometry for each comparison and make sure the cache-on and cache-off arms use the intended GPU paths. This should be a small test-harness and run-configuration change, with a short source inspection to confirm which callback is active.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The main cost is ensuring the comparison is genuinely matched and retaining enough backend evidence in the parity report. It does not require a new numerical kernel, but test setup mistakes can invalidate the result.
scores.quality_comment: A cache-off run could use CPU expert computation, which is a different rounding path, so a mismatch would not by itself prove an upstream GPU-cache defect. The design also explicitly proposes a cached-versus-selective-copy comparison with both paths on GPU; that is a better control. Because the cache-on/off path is not fully specified, record and verify the backend before drawing the claimed conclusion.
scores.urgency_comment: E2b is an early exactness gate, so a path mismatch could cause wasted debugging or a false rejection during M1. The issue is easy to prevent by checking backend traces, and it does not threaten runtime exactness if the matched GPU comparison is used.

scores.time_comment: A useful fix is to define a small synchronous core for first-token readiness, then admit further profile-ranked experts in the background with safe publication and demand priority. Implementing that policy and its slot-lifetime tests is a few days; the design does not require filling the entire bank, so the initial-fill size also needs to be stated.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This adds background transfer scheduling and lease-safe slot publication, but can reuse the planned source and policy interfaces. It is moderate engineering rather than a new inference architecture.
scores.quality_comment: A large ranked warm fill could improve steady-state hits while delaying a short request's first token by seconds if the source is storage-bound. The design measures first-token time but does not specify the warm-fill volume or a deferred-fill policy. Since ranked core need not mean the full 9.16 GiB cache, the magnitude is uncertain and this is a bounded performance opportunity rather than a definite failure.
scores.urgency_comment: The fill is part of P2 and can affect every cold launch, but M1's explicit exit is about hit rate and decode throughput rather than a first-token threshold. It should be measured before shipping, though it need not block the earliest correctness harness.

scores.time_comment: P5a needs a versioned publication sequence in which the slot-map lookup sees the map for the same generation as the corresponding bank contents. Adding and testing that dependency is a several-day change to the proposed event protocol, including delayed-map and delayed-fill tests.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The fix is localized to event ordering and generation management, but it touches both scheduler-visible map reads and asynchronous bank writes. Testing slot reuse under overlapping readers is essential because a simple wait at the matmul is not sufficient.
scores.quality_comment: The graph performs `GET_ROWS` on the slot map before the bank matmul. If the map is stale while the bank has already been overwritten, waiting only at the consumer matmul can pair a valid new bank with an old slot ID and silently compute the wrong expert. P5a's description names a bank-operation wait but not map-publication ordering.
scores.urgency_comment: This matters only if the asynchronous P5a candidate is built, and P5 is scheduled for M2. It should be included in that design before implementation; it does not affect the current synchronous upstream path.

scores.time_comment: Extend E0 and the path-parity harness with the disclosed row counts, capacity edges and representative large-batch selective-copy cases for each layout. The test matrix is a few days of harness work plus runs; it is smaller than developing new kernels.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The workload shapes and layouts are known, so the primary cost is constructing deterministic inputs and capturing intermediate outputs across the relevant paths. It also needs to be maintained when upstream dispatch changes on rebase.
scores.quality_comment: The design calls out distinct dispatch behavior at 7, 8 and 9 rows, yet E0-E2b do not require those row counts or the cache-capacity and large-batch boundaries. Passing one-row or ordinary teacher-forced tests would not establish parity for speculative windows or prefill. This is a real gap in the stated merge gate.
scores.urgency_comment: The row-count boundary is already identified in section 3.3 and affects the exactness claim, so the coverage should be added before E0-E2b are treated as merge gates. It is not an immediate runtime defect while those configurations remain unqualified.

scores.time_comment: The P3 reader specification should discover the relevant platform alignment, round file offsets and lengths outward, read into aligned buffers, and trim to the requested tensor bytes. A robust Windows and Linux implementation with tests against real shard offsets is likely several days.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Direct I/O has different alignment and fallback behavior across operating systems and filesystems. The work is bounded, but the fallback policy must be explicit and measured or the supposedly controlled tail can silently return to buffered page-cache churn.
scores.quality_comment: The design proposes `FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING` and `O_DIRECT` but does not specify aligned reads or a defined fallback. An unaligned expert slice can fail on a supported machine; silently switching to buffered I/O can restore the memory-pressure behavior the tier is intended to avoid. This affects availability and performance more than numerical exactness.
scores.urgency_comment: P3 is scheduled for M2, so there is time to specify and test this before using the source path. It becomes important when supporting Linux, slower drives or shard offsets that do not meet the device's direct-I/O alignment.

scores.time_comment: Separate layout identity from verified model and adapter identity, and version machine timing data by engine/backend configuration, context/KV settings and storage device. This is a few days of profile-schema and invalidation work; hashing can be done once or supplied through a verified manifest rather than on every launch.
scores.cost_effort_comment: There is moderate compatibility work across profile readers, shared routing priors and machine records. Full payload identity can be expensive to calculate for large shards, so the design needs a trusted manifest or cached digest strategy as well as migration behavior.
scores.quality_comment: A tensor-directory hash identifies geometry, not router weights or an adapter that may change which experts are hot. Likewise, a timing profile can become stale after a drive move or execution-configuration change even when the machine fingerprint is unchanged. Local learning and hold-out checks reduce the harm, but the current keys can still make a misleading warm start or plan.
scores.urgency_comment: This matters as soon as profiles are reused or shared and the design explicitly intends a shipped routing prior. It is not an immediate exactness break because placement still computes the selected expert, but it can damage hit-rate predictions and machine-fit decisions.

scores.time_comment: The design can resolve this with a direct policy decision: class D is disabled in the exact default and enabled only by a clearly named non-bitwise option. This is a small documentation and default-configuration change, not a multiweek implementation.
scores.cost_effort_comment: No kernel work is needed to preserve the stated contract. The only coordination is to ensure the launcher, server flags and user-facing mode names do not silently enable speculation in exact mode.
scores.quality_comment: Section 3 defines exactness as bitwise identity, while class D is explicitly not bitwise and section 12 leaves its default open. Distribution-preserving sampling or verified drafts do not guarantee identical logits or a seeded token sequence. Resolving the default protects a fixed project requirement, though the code is not yet stated to enable D.
scores.urgency_comment: This is an open decision rather than a current output defect, but it must be resolved before speculation is wired into a default launch plan. The risk becomes immediate only if class D is enabled while the product is advertised as exact by default.

scores.time_comment: A meaningful support matrix needs at least a real low-VRAM device and a real Linux or slower-link configuration, plus layout and I/O-path tests. Acquiring or borrowing that hardware and maintaining repeatable runs can take several weeks; a memory ballast on the reference GPU cannot substitute for those tests.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This involves hardware access, OS and driver variation, platform-specific direct-I/O and pinning work, and possibly CI or partner-machine coordination. The cost is substantially higher than merely documenting the ballast simulation.
scores.quality_comment: The design honestly labels the 8 GB setup as a ballast simulation and does not promise 85% there, which mitigates the overclaim. But it cannot test another GPU's dispatch, PCIe 3.0 service, Linux I/O alignment or filesystem behavior. If self-calibration is intended to cover these machines, the simulation is a capacity check, not validation of that support claim.
scores.urgency_comment: The gap is important before claiming support beyond the reference laptop, but it does not prevent a narrowly scoped reference-laptop M1 measurement. It becomes urgent when publishing results or enabling the plan on a real low-VRAM or Linux machine.

scores.time_comment: A matched benchmark of seven versus eight total verification rows can be run quickly once the parity rig exists. It should record the actual selected kernels, expert bytes and milliseconds per committed token rather than infer the best cap from eligibility tables.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This is primarily a controlled experiment and a configuration choice. It adds little implementation cost unless the current speculation flags cannot express the desired total-row window.
scores.quality_comment: The design chooses seven rows to keep every Swift layout on MMVQ, while it says eight moves IQ2_S to MMQ and nine sends IQ1_M to fallback. Eight may be slower or faster; there is no evidence either way. Measuring it could recover a small amount of speculative throughput, but it may also show that the conservative cap is best.
scores.urgency_comment: This is an optional class-D tuning opportunity for M3, not a requirement for exact single-token M1 decode. It should wait until the parity and baseline measurements are available.

scores.time_comment: Instrument contiguous upload runs and host submission time after P2, then adjust victim-slot assignment only if fragmentation is material. That measurement and a modest policy change are likely a few days; introducing a separate packed/scatter transfer path would take longer and should not be assumed necessary.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Preserving contiguous source and destination runs is a localized policy constraint. Any staging-and-scatter design adds copies and complexity, so the low-cost first step is to count runs and compare them against the current SLRU behavior.
scores.quality_comment: The source coalesces only adjacent expert IDs assigned to adjacent slots, and P2 does not state how ranked-core or transient placement preserves that property. Fragmentation could cause many small submissions, but the gain is unmeasured and may be small compared with transfer bandwidth and the per-layer drain. CUDA 13 batching evidence also cannot be assumed on the stated CUDA 12.8 toolchain.
scores.urgency_comment: This becomes relevant when the new policy is implemented, but the effect is conditional and likely bounded. Measure it alongside P2/P3 rather than making a speculative transfer subsystem an M1 blocker.

scores.time_comment: The protocol can be corrected by separating cold, controlled-warm and post-prefill tests, counterbalancing arm order, and recording physical reads and starting memory state. This is a small experimental-design change, not a large code project.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The main cost is additional runs and disciplined logging; it may take time to obtain stable measurements because the cache state cannot simply be reset by restarting a process. No engine changes are required.
scores.quality_comment: A fresh process does not clear the operating-system page cache, and each arm can warm or evict different pages for the next arm. Thus identical warm-up text does not guarantee identical page-cache history. Since the supplied measurements vary substantially with memory pressure, the stated ABBA result could confuse cache carryover with an optimization unless starting state and physical I/O are observed.
scores.urgency_comment: This affects the M1.0 and M1.2 performance conclusions, where the design compares against a large noise floor. The per-token hit metric is less sensitive to page-cache state, but decode throughput and the 12 tok/s floor are not.

scores.time_comment: Add conservative automatic limits, deadlines, cleanup and an explicit fallback plan before running the cliff and pinning probes. These safeguards are a few days of implementation and testing; making destructive boundary exploration opt-in is an even smaller policy change.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The probe must manage GPU allocations, RAM availability and commit or cgroup limits, and reliably release resources on timeout or cancellation. This is moderate systems work because a failed cleanup can affect the desktop beyond Marian.
scores.quality_comment: The VRAM probe deliberately allocates until it detects a bandwidth collapse, and the RAM pin test advances in 1 GiB steps. The RAM test mentions an available-memory floor, but the design does not specify a complete safe envelope, commit/cgroup cap, timeout or recovery behavior for the probes. A first-start calibration should not destabilize the constrained machine it is meant to characterize.
scores.urgency_comment: The probes are planned for first-start calibration, so the risk is near-term if they are run automatically. The harm is avoidable with conservative caps and supervision, and the design has not yet been implemented.

scores.time_comment: Specify a versioned schema, atomic replacement, writer coordination and retention of a last-known-good profile. These are conventional persistence changes and should take several days, including tests for interruption and rollback across a rebase.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The code work is modest, but profile compatibility must be considered across engine rebases and concurrent server exits. A small amount of release-process discipline is also needed to retain a compatible binary and plan for rollback.
scores.quality_comment: P4 writes learned counts at exit and the design expects profiles to persist across sessions, but it does not specify atomicity, schema migration or concurrent-writer behavior. A partial or incompatible profile can erase useful learning or create confusing warm-start regressions. Because routing profiles are priors and shared inputs are validated, this is operational reliability rather than a direct numerical-path defect.
scores.urgency_comment: The risk grows after repeated sessions and rebases, rather than blocking the first M1 correctness run. It should be settled before profile persistence becomes routine or shared, but is not as urgent as the live cache and measurement gaps.

scores.time_comment: For M1, the quickest fix is to enforce one qualified active sequence or explicitly define bounded queuing and refusal behavior. Supporting and validating concurrent schedules requires additional row-shape, peak-memory and cancellation tests and is likely about a week of engineering.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The layer must coordinate upstream server settings with cache capacity, request admission and GPU memory. Testing simultaneous requests and refusal/retry behavior is more costly than a single-client benchmark because batching can alter both workspace and `MUL_MAT_ID` geometry.
scores.quality_comment: The contract is conditioned on realized row counts, and the upstream cache path changes with batch size and capacity. A second client can therefore change numerical-path geometry or exceed the calibrated memory envelope. The design says to pause or refuse under pressure but does not define concurrency, queueing or cancellation, so a one-request calibration does not establish ordinary serving behavior.
scores.urgency_comment: This matters when Marian is used through the upstream server, which may receive multiple local requests, and should be made explicit before treating a single-request benchmark as a serving guarantee. It is not necessarily an M1 defect if the launch configuration limits concurrency, but no such limit is currently specified.

scores.time_comment: Define, per layout group and supported row count, how many slots remain available for current misses while the ranked core is protected, and specify when the core can be demoted or selective-copy fallback is used. This is a few days of policy and boundary-test work.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The implementation must coordinate ranked residents, adaptive victims and transient slots without reusing slots still needed by the current operation. The code change is localized, but correctness testing across small budgets and verify windows is necessary.
scores.quality_comment: The design promises that a declined admission still uploads and computes the expert in a transient slot, but does not state a capacity invariant for that slot class or the evictable region. A request can fit the total bank yet lack enough non-core slots if the protected core cannot be demoted in time. The design's adaptive region and selective-copy fallback offer plausible solutions, but their conditions are unspecified.
scores.urgency_comment: This is a P2 policy-design issue and should be resolved before the new core and transient classes are implemented. It is less immediate than a known upstream failure because a correct implementation can demote the core or use the existing large-batch path.

luna.overall_comment: The strongest actionable issues are the fixed-allocation governor (C-02), P5b's unspecified cold-tail service and P5a's map-publication ordering (C-04, C-12), telemetry semantics (C-07), missing row-boundary parity coverage (C-13), incomplete profile invalidation (C-15), and the unresolved class-D default (C-16). C-03 is a material conditional performance risk: P3 is deferred past the decode floor, so M1 should include post-prefill and cold-source endurance tests before assuming the floor is safe. I partly accept C-01 and C-08 because the design already contains relevant safeguards and live checks; C-06 is not a defect as stated because the design explicitly defines row-level hits over 480 lookups rather than requiring reuse of upstream's distinct-expert counter. The remaining findings are mostly bounded implementation, validation or performance opportunities, not evidence that the unrun design has already failed.

scores.time_comment: Specifying payload identity is quick, but verifying shard bytes or a trusted manifest, checking sidecar records and testing replacement files takes roughly a week. The work belongs with P3 before any sidecar is used.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This crosses sidecar generation, loading and failure handling. The refuter cites a section 11 requirement for full identity binding, but that requirement appears in the Astra ideas, not in DESIGN-M1.md; section 6.2's metadata hash covers routing profiles.
scores.quality_comment: Two GGUFs can have identical tensor directories and offsets but different expert payloads. Rejecting a stale derived sidecar prevents silently supplying wrong weights, which directly protects the design's bitwise exactness contract.
scores.urgency_comment: The current upstream fill uses the original tensor, so this is not an immediate M1.1 failure. It becomes urgent before M2 enables the optional expert-major sidecar.

scores.time_comment: A supervised restart into a smaller, parity-qualified bank may take about a week. Truly reclaimable bank segments, graph rebinding and safe reader draining would take longer; M1 should choose and implement one route explicitly.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The bank buffer is allocated at construction in llama-moe-cache.cpp:388-470. Changing slot occupancy cannot free it, so the proposed M1.3 competing-allocation test needs process control or substantial cache-allocation changes.
scores.quality_comment: Physical reclamation could avoid the documented several-fold performance cliff or an OOM when another process takes VRAM. Pausing admission and logically shrinking the adaptive region alone do not accomplish the stated governor behavior.
scores.urgency_comment: The reference Windows laptop has already shown a sharp near-capacity slowdown, and the unsupported governor is an M1.3 exit criterion. The precise cliff under this new pin remains unmeasured.

scores.time_comment: Adding post-prefill endurance measurements is a short task; advancing a bounded source into M1 means implementing and testing staging, RAM accounting and both copy paths, likely one to several weeks.
scores.cost_effort_comment: P3 is deliberately scheduled for M2, so advancing it changes the milestone and involves I/O, memory budgeting and cache integration. It should be conditional on a matched pinned-build test, not on attributing the older slowdown to paging as fact.
scores.quality_comment: At an illustrative 85% byte hit rate, roughly 99 MiB of expert bytes still miss per token. Avoiding faults in those misses could materially improve sustained decode, but neither the new pin's speed nor the gain from a source tier has been measured.
scores.urgency_comment: M1's 12 tok/s floor makes this a near-term falsifier. First test cold and post-pp4096/16K decode; implement the earlier source only if the measured floor or stability requires it.

scores.time_comment: P5b needs a concurrent, intra-token demand channel, reader wake-up, mapped-memory ordering, errors and a safe fallback. Designing and stress-testing that protocol is multiweek work, unless P5a is selected instead.
scores.cost_effort_comment: This is more than admission-policy bookkeeping: the GPU cannot finish the waiting token until a host worker learns which NVMe expert to fetch. Cross-device synchronization and failure recovery make the implementation risky.
scores.quality_comment: P5b describes draining its miss ring between tokens while a cold-tail miss waits during the current token. A timeout limits a hang but does not produce the missing exact expert bytes; the specified path can fail exact execution.
scores.urgency_comment: P5 is deferred to M2 and selected after measurements, so no current M1 run is blocked. The demand protocol must be settled before choosing P5b for a machine with an NVMe tail.

scores.time_comment: Adding tracing at a shared router point or in the selective-copy path, then validating row and phase counts against pp4096, is several days of patching and tests.
scores.cost_effort_comment: P1 names llama_moe_cache::copy() as its ID hook, but get_slot_map() bypasses that hook for large batches at :496-507. The separately mentioned pre-P1 eval callback is not specified as P1/P4's continuing prefill source.
scores.quality_comment: A 20k-token corpus dominated by prefill could otherwise produce incomplete prefill counts while appearing to provide phase-specific profiles. Covering both paths makes replay and subsequent budget choices interpretable.
scores.urgency_comment: P1 and routing-profile construction are M1.1 work. Missing most large-ubatch selections would contaminate calibration before the M1.2 policy is assessed.

scores.time_comment: Documenting separate row-lookup and distinct-fill counters, then testing a duplicate-ID multirow trace, should take a few days. No cache redesign is necessary.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The source fact is clear: plan() de-duplicates IDs at :109-152 before incrementing n_hit. The refuter is also right that the design asks for per-token IDs and does not expressly reuse that upstream counter as its lookup numerator.
scores.quality_comment: An explicit pre-admission, per-row residency count prevents a plausible implementation mistake in verify-window reporting. The ordinary single-token 480-lookup target is less exposed because top-k IDs within a row are distinct.
scores.urgency_comment: The distinction matters when P1's metrics are implemented and especially when speculation is evaluated. It is not evidence that the written design already reports a false M1 single-token hit rate.

scores.time_comment: Defining and instrumenting routing completion, host planning, transfer completion and consumer readiness takes several days. A callback-duration counter alone cannot deliver the promised bank-ready timestamp.
scores.cost_effort_comment: At :582-584 the callback waits before planning, while :591-614 only submits asynchronous writes. Separating preceding GPU work from exposed cache work requires host tracing plus appropriately placed GPU events and low-overhead controls.
scores.quality_comment: M1.0 uses drain timing to prioritize P5, and P1 promises exposed-wait measurements. Mislabeling synchronization duration or upload submission as bank-ready time could send substantial optimization work in the wrong direction.
scores.urgency_comment: The drain measurement is one of the first experiments, before P1 exists. Its event definitions should be fixed immediately so the subsequent policy and scheduling decisions use comparable measurements.

scores.time_comment: Adding loaded-server validation at requested context, peak ubatch and controlled competition, with finer investigation near a suspected boundary, is several days of probe and test work.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The refuter correctly notes that section 7 already budgets KV/workspace and includes a short live confirmation and a competing-allocation test. The remaining gap is whether those limited checks qualify a sustained, peak-memory serving workload.
scores.quality_comment: A model-free 256 MiB-step cliff probe cannot alone identify every server peak or growth effect. Stronger live qualification reduces the chance of a several-fold slowdown, without claiming that the older runs' 22 MiB peak difference measured a precise threshold.
scores.urgency_comment: This matters for M1.3 planning, but existing live checks partially mitigate it. Measure their adequacy on the pinned build before treating the standalone probe as either sufficient or useless.

scores.time_comment: Formalizing operation-level equivalence and broad Swift-shape coverage takes at least a week. Obtaining a suitable large GPU for an additional end-to-end run may take longer and still would not be the reference laptop's same-GPU oracle.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Swift's 33.02 GiB routed experts alone exceed the laptop's 16 GB VRAM. E0, a smaller model and two Swift GPU paths are useful tests, but none literally runs the stipulated whole-Swift all-resident reference on that GPU.
scores.quality_comment: A stated per-operation equivalence obligation and dispatch-coverage matrix would make the evidence honest and much stronger. Passing surrogate runs should not be described as direct proof of an unavailable whole-model reference.
scores.urgency_comment: Exactness is an M1 exit criterion, so the scope of its evidence must be decided before calling E0-E2b a passing gate. This is a validation limitation, not proof that cached Swift outputs differ.

scores.time_comment: Inspecting operation backend and row-count traces and restricting the comparison to two confirmed GPU paths should take hours to a couple of days.
scores.cost_effort_comment: E2b separately proposes a GPU selective-copy comparison and an upstream cache-on/off check. The latter does not establish that cache-off host weights use GPU rather than CPU expert kernels.
scores.quality_comment: CPU and GPU expert computation can differ in last bits for an expected reason. Identifying the actual backend prevents a correct bank path from being rejected or an upstream cache defect from being misdiagnosed.
scores.urgency_comment: The cache-on/off check is scheduled for M1.0 as an early exactness decision. Its interpretation should be corrected before those first results are recorded.

scores.time_comment: A synchronous-small-core experiment is quick; safe demand-prioritized background filling and publication require several days of P2 and launcher work.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Section 4 explicitly fills the ranked core before the first token, but gives neither its size nor a startup budget. Deferred fill must respect active readers and avoid allowing speculative work to delay demand.
scores.quality_comment: On a cold short request, avoiding an illustrative 8 GiB of unnecessary reads at 2 GiB/s could remove about four seconds of startup I/O. Steady-state decode may improve little or even suffer initially, so measure TTFT and later hits together.
scores.urgency_comment: Warm fill is part of M1's policy work and first-token time is already a metric. Its size-dependent harm is plausible, not established until a cold-start test on the actual source is run.

scores.time_comment: Adding generation-aware dependencies for both map lookup and bank consumption, plus delayed-copy and eviction stress tests, is approximately a week's work within P5a.
scores.cost_effort_comment: P5a specifies the bank operation waiting on copy completion, whereas the existing GET_ROWS consumes the slot map earlier. Event placement, map versions and reader leases must agree across scheduler splits.
scores.quality_comment: If GET_ROWS sees an old map and the matmul waits for newly filled contents at that slot, it may compute a different expert without an obvious error. Ordering the lookup as well as the bank protects exactness.
scores.urgency_comment: P5a is deferred and conditional on drain measurements. Nevertheless this ordering must be an acceptance condition before any asynchronous version enters exact mode.

scores.time_comment: A parameterized parity matrix over rows, layouts, capacity fallbacks and actual prefill ubatches is several days of harness work, followed by GPU test time.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Section 3.3 identifies the 7-, 8- and 9-row dispatch changes, yet E0-E2b prescribe no corresponding shape matrix. Generated-token parity and 512 teacher-forced tokens do not guarantee those particular MUL_MAT_ID calls occur.
scores.quality_comment: Testing 1, 7, 8, 9 and 32 rows and the large-batch path targets precisely where kernel or cache-path changes might defeat the bitwise claim. It also makes failures reproducible at intermediate outputs.
scores.urgency_comment: E0-E2b are merge gates from M1.0 onward. The matrix should precede any claim that later verify-window or prefill configurations are covered by those gates.

scores.time_comment: Implementing alignment discovery, outward-rounded reads, trimmed bounce buffers and tested fallback on Windows and Linux takes several days within P3.
scores.cost_effort_comment: P3 names FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING and O_DIRECT without specifying buffer, offset or length alignment. Fable's supplied idea explicitly identifies sector-rounding work for GGUF offsets, so this is an identifiable design omission rather than an observed bug.
scores.quality_comment: The contract prevents cold experts from failing to load or silently returning to uncontrolled buffered reads on an unlike machine. It is especially useful for the low-RAM tail, while leaving the expert bytes unchanged.
scores.urgency_comment: No P3 reader exists in M1. The handling should be settled before M2 claims portable unbuffered sourcing, not treated as a present decode regression.

scores.time_comment: Adding verified model/adapter identity and versioned timing keys, plus invalidation tests, is several days; obtaining or checking full-shard digests can add startup work unless a trusted manifest exists.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Section 6.2 hashes tensor information and offsets, which do not identify changed router payloads. Its stated re-probe triggers also omit explicit engine-build, KV-setting and model-drive changes, despite those affecting service timings or workspace.
scores.quality_comment: A same-layout fine-tune can inherit the wrong popularity ranking, and a moved model can inherit obsolete disk measurements. Better keys improve warm-hit predictions and make profile reuse explainable; wrong routing ranks do not themselves change expert arithmetic.
scores.urgency_comment: Profiles are constructed and reused during M1, so model identity needs early attention. The additional machine-timing keys become particularly important when P3's storage tier is enabled.

scores.time_comment: Resolving the rule in the mode specification and launcher defaults takes hours. Verification then needs a small configuration test proving class-D switches remain disabled in exact mode.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Nothing says class D is enabled today; it is an open question for Chris. But section 3 explicitly calls it non-bitwise, so allowing it as the default conflicts with the brief's already fixed exact-by-default decision.
scores.quality_comment: Declaring class D opt-in for the exact preset prevents distribution-preserving speculation from being mistaken for bitwise-identical logits and seeded tokens. This does not criticize the intentionally disabled, answer-changing class-A switches.
scores.urgency_comment: The ambiguity can be removed now at little cost. Its practical harm arises only if a future launcher chooses the non-bitwise branch as its advertised exact default.

scores.time_comment: Qualifying a real lower-VRAM GPU, Linux I/O, a slower link or drive, and another layout requires hardware access and multiweek testing. The quicker fix is to label the existing ballast experiment narrowly.
scores.cost_effort_comment: A VRAM ballast and RAM cap preserve the 4090's kernels, PCIe path, Windows storage APIs and much of its allocation behavior. They cannot establish the design's broad self-calibration claim for those unlike machines.
scores.quality_comment: A supported matrix with measured degraded or refusal outcomes prevents capacity simulation from being mistaken for cross-platform validation. The design appropriately avoids promising 85% hits on 8 GB; the gap is proof that its mechanism works there.
scores.urgency_comment: M1.3 uses the simulated class as a validation exit, so its label must be corrected then. Real-hardware qualification is urgent before general availability, not necessarily before reference-laptop experimentation.

scores.time_comment: An opt-in seven-versus-eight-total-row sweep on high-acceptance prompts should take a day or two after speculation is available.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The seven-row cap deliberately keeps all listed layouts on MMVQ, while the eighth moves IQ2_S to MMQ and the ninth introduces the IQ1_M fallback. Measuring eight is worthwhile, but omitting it is not a proven speed loss.
scores.quality_comment: An eighth row might amortize fixed work on favorable prompts, with an illustrative 0-10% upside, or lose to the kernel switch and extra misses. This layer-on-top class-D experiment cannot be sold as bitwise-exact acceleration.
scores.urgency_comment: Speculation is M3 and its default remains unresolved. The measurement is low priority relative to M1 residency, exactness and sustained decode.

scores.time_comment: Counting upload runs and submission time is a small instrumentation task; testing contiguous victim choices or packed unchanged-byte staging takes several additional days.
scores.cost_effort_comment: At :591-605 uploads coalesce only when expert IDs and assigned slots are both consecutive. P2 introduces more slot classes without saying how they retain that property, but fragmentation and a useful CUDA 12.8 remedy remain unmeasured.
scores.quality_comment: At roughly 72 misses for an illustrative 85% of 480 lookups, three tensor roles can create many submissions even when bytes fall. Preserving coalescing could give a bounded decode gain, plausibly 0-5%, if submission time is exposed.
scores.urgency_comment: Instrument during P2 so a better hit curve is not accepted while submission stalls worsen. Do not prioritize a batching implementation solely from the CUDA-13 microbenchmark.

scores.time_comment: Reworking the run protocol into measured cold, controlled-warm and post-prefill conditions, with counterbalanced order and starting-state checks, takes several days of automation and repeated tests.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Fresh process exit does not clear OS cached file pages. An identical nominal warm-up also cannot guarantee equal history when the arms read or evict different expert pages; ABBA ordering reduces some drift but does not prove equivalence.
scores.quality_comment: Recording physical reads, faults and memory state prevents cache carryover from being mistaken for a throughput gain or loss. That matters given the older baseline's large variation, although its cause was not experimentally isolated.
scores.urgency_comment: Section 9.3's asserted equal page-cache history underpins the first pinned-build comparisons and the 12 tok/s decision. Correct the claim and protocol before performance results are interpreted.

scores.time_comment: Adding conservative allocation ceilings, child-process deadlines, cleanup and fallback behavior is a several-day probe change. Destructive boundary exploration can be a separately supervised diagnostic.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The automatic approximately 90-second probe includes deliberate cliff exploration and 1 GiB pin increments. An available-memory floor is some protection, but no probe-specific timeout, cancellation, commit or container-bound rule is stated.
scores.quality_comment: A resource envelope improves first-use reliability on the constrained laptops being targeted. It avoids destabilizing the desktop merely to discover a plan, without changing model outputs or directly raising cache hits.
scores.urgency_comment: This becomes relevant when M1.3 automates first-start calibration. It should be built before ordinary users run the probes, rather than after an observed memory-pressure incident.

scores.time_comment: Atomic versioned publication, writer coordination and last-known-good selection take several days; bounded incremental checkpoints and full binary rollback add further work.
scores.cost_effort_comment: P4 dumps counts at exit and the fork rebases fortnightly, but the design specifies no atomic update or compatibility rules. A crash need not corrupt an existing file—it may merely lose learning—so the failure modes should be distinguished.
scores.quality_comment: Versioning and safe publication prevent profile corruption and make regressions recoverable. They chiefly improve operational reliability and reproducibility rather than immediate decode speed.
scores.urgency_comment: Persistent counts arrive in M1.3, when basic atomicity should be present. A fuller last-known-good binary-and-plan bundle is important before routine rebases or wider deployment.

scores.time_comment: Enforcing and testing one active sequence for M1 is roughly a week's server-launch and request-outcome work. Qualifying concurrent row schedules and peak allocations instead would take longer.
scores.cost_effort_comment: The design launches upstream llama-server and promises to pause admission, but defines no M1 concurrency limit, bounded queue or refusal behavior. Cache eligibility itself changes with token count and available slots at :496-507.
scores.quality_comment: An explicit serving envelope makes calibrated memory peaks and same-row-count parity claims meaningful for real requests. It also gives clients a defined outcome under memory pressure rather than an indefinite pause.
scores.urgency_comment: Server prompts are part of M1 measurement and M1.3 tests competing memory use. Qualify or constrain concurrency before treating single-request results as serving guarantees.

scores.time_comment: Adding a per-group capacity invariant, safe immediate demotion or an early selective-copy fallback, with all-core-cold tests, is several days within P2.
scores.cost_effort_comment: Upstream checks a request against total group slots, not a newly protected core plus evictable remainder. The proposed hysteretic demotion does not say what happens when more cold experts arrive than transient and adaptive slots can hold.
scores.quality_comment: The invariant ensures an eligible exact request can still assign one usable slot per selected expert. Without it, a small bank or verify window can abort despite passing the existing total-capacity check.
scores.urgency_comment: This is a P2 policy-design issue, before the ranked core is merged in M1.2. Its failure is conditional on core size and requests, but cold-selection stress tests can expose it early.

sol.overall_comment: The strongest immediate findings concern M1's non-reclaiming governor, incomplete large-batch tracing, timing definitions and performance controls. Exactness risks in the proposed asynchronous paths need explicit ordering and demand-service protocols before M2. The pin has no GPU performance results, so paging losses and proposed speedups remain hypotheses to test. The refuter's proposed DESIGN-M1.md sidecar safeguard is not present in the supplied design; conversely, the design does not explicitly misuse upstream's de-duplicated counters.

final.summary: Prioritise trustworthy M1 measurements and exactness gates, then make the memory-pressure response and serving limits implementable. The pinned build has not been benchmarked, so the proposed performance gains remain hypotheses. All 24 collated items are retained.
final.ordering: I ranked every item by the two judges’ mean quality plus mean urgency, highest first; ties go to lower combined mean time and cost. Each item’s why gives its means as quality/urgency/time/cost. Time and cost are the judges’ relative scores, not days. Deferred M2 correctness risks retain their high quality scores but rank below equally valuable M1 work because their urgency is lower. No item qualified for removal under the refuter-versus-judge rule. C-01, C-06 and C-08 are refuter_unverifiable: they remain in the value ranking, but access and clarification work belongs solely in brief_author_plan, not action_plan. C-06 is ranked for completeness although the proposed design defect is rejected. There are no collator-REFUTED items to place last.

items.title: P1 does not define a valid bank-ready or exposed-wait timestamp
items.why: Means 8.5/7.5/4.5/5. The callback synchronizes before planning but only submits asynchronous fills afterward. Callback duration is neither bank-ready time nor avoidable drain time, yet M1.0 uses it to decide P5’s priority.
items.fix: Define routing-complete, planning, submission, transfer-complete and consumer-ready events; calculate exposed critical-path wait. Report dropped traces and compare instrumentation-on with off.

items.title: The parity gate does not enumerate the kernel row-count boundaries it identifies
items.why: Means 8.5/6.5/4.5/4.5. E0–E2b do not require the identified 7-, 8- and 9-row dispatch cases or cache-capacity and large-batch boundaries. A one-row pass cannot qualify those paths.
items.fix: Parameterize parity tests for 1, 7, 8, 9 and 32 rows, capacity fallback, large-batch selective copy and actual prefill ubatches across all three Swift layouts; compare intermediate outputs and logits.

items.title: Identical warm-up in fresh processes does not equalize page-cache history
items.why: Means 7.5/7/3.5/4. Process exit retains OS-cached pages, and one arm may warm or displace the next arm’s data. This can distort the decode floor and apparent optimisation gains; the older slowdown’s cause is not proven.
items.fix: Separate cold, controlled-warm and post-prefill runs; counterbalance order, freeze learning, log starting memory state, physical reads and faults, and repeat A–A controls.
items.judges_disagree: The judges agree on the defect but differ by three points on time: Luna expects a small protocol correction; Sol includes several days of automation and repeated runs.

items.title: The M1 governor cannot physically shrink upstream's fixed bank
items.why: Means 8/6.5/6.5/7.5. The bank is allocated at construction. Invalidating slots or pausing admission cannot reclaim VRAM, so the promised M1.3 response to a competing allocation cannot pass as written.
items.fix: Choose either supervised restart into a smaller parity-qualified plan or genuinely reclaimable bank segments with safe reader draining and graph rebinding. Test recovered driver-budget usage, not merely slot occupancy.

items.title: PERF: Put a minimal bounded expert source before the M1 throughput exit
items.why: Means 8/6/7/8. P3 is deferred although M1 requires sustained 12 tok/s. At an illustrative 85% byte hit rate, about 99 MiB/token still misses; storage service could dominate, but neither paging causality nor failure on the new pin is measured. The byte-preserving remedy could have no gain without paging or recover a substantial post-prefill slowdown.
items.fix: First run matched cold and pp4096/16K-to-decode endurance tests. If the floor or stability fails, advance bounded RAM, pinned staging and queued tail sourcing into M1, covering both small-cache fills and large-batch copies. Put source hooks in llama.cpp and tier management above it.

items.title: The class-D default remains unresolved despite exact-by-default
items.verdict: Unresolved default conflicts with the fixed contract
items.why: Means 8.5/5/1.5/1.5. Class D is explicitly non-bitwise, so allowing it as the advertised exact default would violate a settled requirement. Neither judge says it is already enabled.
items.fix: Make class D off in the exact launch preset; give it an explicit non-bitwise option and test launcher defaults separately from its quality gate.
items.judges_disagree: Luna says yes and Sol partly: both see the policy conflict, but Sol stresses that this is an open decision, not an observed output defect.

items.title: Serving concurrency and memory-pressure admission are undefined
items.why: Means 8/5.5/5.5/6. Another local request can change row geometry, cache path and peak workspace. The design promises to pause or refuse requests without defining queue, timeout, cancellation or refusal outcomes.
items.fix: For M1, enforce one qualified active sequence or qualify concurrent schedules. Define bounded queuing and refusal through upstream-server facilities; test realized rows, peak allocations and request outcomes.

items.title: The Swift parity gate lacks its literal same-GPU all-resident oracle
items.verdict: Confirmed limitation of the exactness evidence
items.why: Means 8/5.5/6.5/7. Swift’s 33.02 GiB of routed experts cannot fit on the reference 16 GB GPU. E0, another model and Swift GPU-path comparisons are useful surrogates, not the literal whole-Swift reference.
items.fix: State a per-operation equivalence obligation and its compositional assumptions, backed by the dispatch and shape matrix. Add a larger-GPU whole-Swift comparison where feasible, without calling it the reference laptop’s same-GPU oracle.
items.judges_disagree: Luna partly agrees because the design acknowledges the missing oracle and supplies surrogate gates; Sol agrees that those gates cannot directly prove the literal contract.

items.title: A cache-off Swift comparison may not isolate an upstream cache exactness defect
items.why: Means 6.5/6.5/2.5/3. Cache-off host weights might execute on CPU rather than through GPU selective copy. Expected CPU/GPU last-bit differences would not prove a defective bank path.
items.fix: Record each compared expert operation’s backend, kernel and row count. Use two confirmed GPU paths for the bank/selective-copy parity claim; label CPU comparisons separately.
items.judges_disagree: Luna partly agrees because E2b also proposes a sound GPU selective-copy control; Sol agrees the additional cache-on/off claim needs qualification. Their quality and urgency scores each differ by three points.

items.title: The proposed cache callback misses large-batch prefill routing
items.verdict: Confirmed P1/P4 coverage gap, partly mitigated by an existing callback
items.why: Means 7/6/4.5/5. Above 32 tokens or the slot-capacity bound, routing bypasses the proposed cache copy() trace. A prefill-heavy calibration could therefore persist incomplete phase counts.
items.fix: Use a shared router trace or instrument the selective-copy path as well. Preserve row and phase identity for P1 and P4, and require expected selection counts on pp4096.
items.judges_disagree: Luna partly agrees because the design already names an eval callback that can capture routing; Sol agrees because it is not specified as P1/P4’s continuing large-batch source.

items.title: Routing and timing profiles omit content and configuration invalidation
items.why: Means 7/5.5/4.5/5. Tensor metadata and offsets do not identify changed router weights; a moved model, changed build or KV setting can also make reused timing estimates stale. Wrong ranks hurt predictions, not expert arithmetic.
items.fix: Separate layout identity from verified model and adapter payload identity. Key timing plans by build, backend, KV/context configuration and storage device; log each reuse or invalidation reason.

items.title: P5a must order slot-map lookup, not just the bank matmul
items.verdict: Plausible exactness defect in the deferred async design
items.why: Means 9.5/3/5/6. GET_ROWS precedes the bank matmul. Waiting only at the matmul could combine an old slot ID with newly overwritten bank contents and silently compute the wrong expert.
items.fix: Gate map lookup on publication of its generation and bank consumption on the matching fill; use reader leases and stress delayed writes and reuse before enabling P5a.
items.judges_disagree: Both agree on the risk; Luna rates it High and Sol Critical. They agree it is conditional on the M2 implementation, rather than a present upstream failure.

items.title: P5b has no specified intra-token host service for a cold tail miss
items.verdict: Confirmed liveness and exactness gap in the deferred alternative
items.why: Means 9.5/3/7.5/9. A layer waiting on a cold NVMe expert cannot finish if the host learns of its demand only from a between-token miss-ring drain. A timeout does not supply the bytes.
items.fix: Prefer P5a for cold tails initially. Before enabling P5b, specify intra-token demand publication, a concurrent reader, byte/flag ordering, errors and an exact timeout fallback; force cold misses and I/O errors in tests.
items.judges_disagree: Both agree on the failure; Luna rates it High and Sol Critical. Its low current urgency reflects that P5b is an optional M2 alternative.

items.title: Protected-core policy needs an explicit transient-capacity invariant
items.why: Means 7/5/4/4.5. Upstream checks total group slots, not how many remain evictable after adding a protected core. A cold selected set could fit the bank yet lack usable transient slots.
items.fix: Specify evictable capacity per group and supported row count, safe immediate core demotion and an early selective-copy fallback; test all-core-cold selections before merging P2.
items.judges_disagree: Both agree it needs a policy invariant; Luna rates the conditional gap Medium and Sol High because an unhandled request could abort.

items.title: A ballast and RAM cap do not validate unlike machines
items.why: Means 7.5/4.5/8.5/8.5. The proposed simulation retains the 4090’s kernels and link and Windows I/O. It can test capacity, not Linux, a real 8 GB GPU, PCIe 3.0, a slower drive or another layout.
items.fix: Label ballast results capacity-only. Set a supported-machine matrix, real-hardware and alternative-layout qualification, and explicit degraded, unsupported or refusal outcomes before claiming broad self-calibration.

items.title: Automatic limit probes lack a safe resource envelope
items.why: Means 6/5/3.5/4.5. Automatic cliff exploration and 1 GiB pinning steps have an available-memory floor but no complete timeout, cancellation, commit/cgroup ceiling or recovery rule.
items.fix: Cap automatic probes conservatively; supervise allocations with deadlines and cleanup, and retain a conservative fallback plan. Make destructive boundary exploration an opt-in diagnostic.

items.title: A coarse standalone VRAM probe cannot certify the serving budget
items.verdict: Partly substantiated; existing live checks narrow the gap
items.why: Means 6.5/4.5/4.5/4.5. A model-free 256 MiB-step probe cannot reproduce every server peak, but the design already budgets context/workspace and confirms finalists live. The refuter makes that counterargument; both judges still want explicit peak-context and competing-load qualification. The refuter’s asserted document access could not be verified, so ownership remains with the brief author.
items.fix: Widen access to the complete design and research pack, then require loaded-server checks at requested context, peak ubatch and controlled competition, refining the boundary and recording OOM and headroom.
items.owner_action: widen access to ../DESIGN-M1.md; ../RESEARCH-PACK.md, then re-run once

items.title: PERF: Avoid making the entire ranked warm fill a first-token barrier
items.why: Means 5.5/4.5/4.5/4.5. The core’s fill size is unspecified. At an illustrative 2 GiB/s, deferring an unnecessary 8 GiB read could save about four seconds of cold-start I/O; steady-state gain may be zero or initially negative. This is exact placement-only work.
items.fix: In llama.cpp P2 and the Marian launch plan, compare full warm fill with a small synchronous core and demand-prioritized, lease-safe background fill. Measure cold TTFT and subsequent hits together.
items.judges_disagree: Luna partly agrees because the core need not occupy the whole bank; Sol agrees that its unspecified size can create a first-token barrier. Neither treats the four-second illustration as measured.

items.title: Bind expert sidecars to payload bytes, not just tensor metadata
items.verdict: Partly substantiated specification gap; brief-author owned
items.why: Means 7/2.5/4/4. A shape-compatible stale sidecar could break bitwise exactness. The refuter argues that a full-identity safeguard already exists in design section 11 and that the metadata hash is only for routing profiles. Sol finds that quoted safeguard in the ideas, not DESIGN-M1.md; Luna sees an already recognised risk but wants payload-level detail. The refuter’s asserted access could not be verified. No sidecar is in M1.
items.fix: The brief author should make the complete design and cited materials accessible and establish which text is authoritative. Specify verified source-payload identity, sidecar-record checks, atomic publication and mismatch refusal before optional P3 sidecars are enabled.
items.judges_disagree: Luna partly agrees and scores quality 4; Sol agrees and scores 10. They differ by six quality points and four on both time and cost because Luna views this chiefly as clarification, while Sol includes implementation and payload verification.
items.owner_action: widen access to ../DESIGN-M1.md, then re-run once

items.title: Learned profiles and fortnightly rebases lack crash-safe rollback rules
items.why: Means 5.5/3.5/4.5/4.5. P4 writes counts at exit without specified atomicity, concurrent-writer rules or compatibility across rebases. A crash may simply lose learning; a partial or incompatible publication has a greater recovery cost.
items.fix: Version and atomically replace profiles, coordinate writers and test interruption. Retain a last-known-good compatible binary, plan and profile for rollback.

items.title: Unbuffered expert reads need an explicit alignment and fallback contract
items.why: Means 6/3/4.5/5. Direct I/O requires appropriate offset, length and buffer alignment; unspecified failure or silent buffered fallback could break cold reads or restore page-cache churn on another machine.
items.fix: In the P3 source, discover platform alignment, round reads outward into aligned buffers, trim to exact expert bytes and make bounded, measured buffered fallback explicit. Test real shard offsets on Windows and Linux.

items.title: PERF: Preserve coalescing and measure fill-submission overhead
items.why: Means 4.5/3.5/4/4. Uploads merge only when source expert IDs and destination slots are consecutive; P2 could fragment them. An exact placement or transfer change might yield 0–5% decode gain, but neither exposed submission cost nor a CUDA 12.8 batching remedy is established. Revive if P2 traces show material exposed submission time or a regression despite better hit rates.
items.fix: Count upload runs and submission microseconds in the llama.cpp P2/P3 path. Only then test contiguous eligible-slot choices or unchanged-byte packed staging; do not assume CUDA-13 microbenchmark gains.
items.judges_disagree: Both partly agree; Luna rates the likely bounded effect Low, while Sol rates it Medium pending measurement.

items.title: Distinct-expert cache counters are not row-level lookup hits
items.verdict: Upstream counter fact confirmed; alleged design defect rejected
items.why: Means 3.5/2.5/2.5/2.5. Upstream plan() counts distinct experts, so that counter would misstate multirow lookup hits if reused. The refuter notes that the design instead specifies per-token IDs and hits over 480 selections; Luna finds no stated misuse, and Sol sees only an implementation precaution. The refuter’s asserted design access could not be verified, so the item remains ranked and brief-author owned rather than procedurally refuted.
items.fix: No design correction established. The brief author should expose the authoritative P1 metric specification and add a duplicate-ID check distinguishing pre-admission row hits from distinct fills.
items.judges_disagree: Luna says no; Sol partly agrees as a preventative check. Quality differs by five points, and urgency, time and cost each by three. Both reject a claim that the written M1 single-token metric is already wrong.
items.owner_action: widen access to ../DESIGN-M1.md, then re-run once

items.title: PERF: Measure eight total verification rows before capping at seven
items.why: Means 3/2/2.5/2. The eighth row moves IQ2_S to MMQ but avoids the identified nine-row IQ1_M fallback. It might yield 0–10% on favourable high-acceptance work or regress. Revive in M3 after opt-in speculation and its parity rig are available; this is not bitwise-exact M1 acceleration.
items.fix: In the layer on top, benchmark seven versus eight total verify rows using kernels, expert bytes and milliseconds per committed token; retain the better qualified cap.
items.judges_disagree: Luna agrees it merits a test; Sol partly agrees because omitting that test is not a demonstrated speed loss.

final.action_plan: Change request 1 — make M1 evidence credible: implement completion-aware timing and trace integrity (C-07), the row/layout/capacity parity matrix and honest Swift oracle claim (C-13, C-09), verify GPU backends in E2b (C-10), cover large-batch routing in P1/P4 (C-05), and replace assumed equal page-cache history with measured cold, warm and post-prefill protocols (C-20). Change request 2 — make the M1 serving envelope real: select a physical bank-reclamation or supervised-restart response (C-02), constrain concurrency and define request outcomes (C-23), establish P2’s transient-capacity invariant (C-24), turn class D off in the exact default (C-16), and bound automatic probes (C-21). Change request 3 — protect sustained performance and profiles: run C-03’s pinned-build endurance falsifier, advancing minimal sourcing only if needed for M1; correct profile identity and invalidation (C-15), measure staged warm fill (C-11), and add crash-safe profile publication (C-22). Change request 4 — gate M2 I/O and async work: specify aligned, bounded direct-I/O fallback (C-14); require matching map and bank generations for P5a (C-12); and do not enable P5b with a cold tail until intra-token host demand service and exact failure behavior exist (C-04). Change request 5 — qualify broader deployment with real unlike hardware rather than ballast alone (C-17). C-19 and C-18 remain measurement-triggered experiments, not committed speedups. C-01, C-06 and C-08 are deliberately excluded from these solution-author change requests.
final.brief_author_plan: For refuter_unverifiable C-01, C-06 and C-08, widen access to the actual DESIGN-M1.md and cited research pack and record which text the refuter reviewed. Resolve C-01’s conflicting claim about whether payload-level sidecar binding is already specified; publish an authoritative requirement before sidecars are used. For C-06, expose the intended row-level metric and a duplicate-ID acceptance check, without claiming a current miscount. For C-08, make explicit whether live confirmation must exercise requested context, peak ubatch and competing allocations. Keep these three out of the solution-author action plan until that access and scope work is complete.
